title: Site Uptime
text:
The rolling-window uptime percentage for each monitored CanadaLogin site, showing what proportion of five-minute pings succeeded over each time horizon.
Six sites are monitored: the two public-facing login pages (EN/FR), the Manage Profile app (staging and production), and the IdP (staging and production).

title: Site Uptime
text:
Calculation
Filter to the most recent date partition and read the precomputed rolling-window uptime columns from sre.uptime_summary. Each uptime_* column is already a percentage (0-100), calculated from all five-minute pings over the named window.
To track uptime over time for a specific site, remove the MAX(date) filter and group by date.






Warning



Upstream monitoring gap (July 28 – September 23, 2026): External synthetic health checks in cds-snc/status-statut halted during this ~8-week window. Because zero down minutes were recorded across zero executed pings, sre.uptime_summary defaulted to reporting uptime_day = 100.0% with response_day_ms = 0.

When aggregating daily uptime or querying historical trends, filter out unmonitored days using WHERE response_day_ms > 0.
In snapshot queries, treat response_day_ms = 0 (or NULL) as unmonitored rather than confirmed 100% availability.









NoteExample queries






SQLR


Latest snapshot, all sites, all rolling windows:
SELECT
    slug,
    lang,
    status,
    uptime_day,
    uptime_week,
    uptime_month,
    uptime_year,
    uptime_alltime
FROM sre.uptime_summary
WHERE date = (SELECT MAX(date) FROM sre.uptime_summary)
ORDER BY slug;
Trend over time, year uptime for a specific site:
SELECT
    date,
    uptime_year,
    uptime_alltime
FROM sre.uptime_summary
-- set the reporting window; see the timespans note in cookbook/notes.qmd
WHERE slug = 'canada-login-website-en'
  AND CAST(date AS DATE) BETWEEN DATE '2026-01-01' AND DATE '2026-06-30'
  -- exclude dates where upstream monitoring was inactive
  AND response_day_ms > 0
ORDER BY date;


Latest snapshot, all sites, all rolling windows:
uptime_s <- tbl(con, in_schema("sre", "uptime_summary"))
latest_date <- uptime_s |> summarise(d = max(date, na.rm = TRUE)) |> pull(d)

uptime_s |>
  filter(as.Date(date) == as.Date(latest_date)) |>
  select(slug, lang, status, uptime_day, uptime_week, uptime_month,
         uptime_year, uptime_alltime) |>
  arrange(slug)
Trend over time, year uptime for a specific site:
tbl(con, in_schema("sre", "uptime_summary")) |>
  # set the reporting window; see the timespans note in cookbook/notes.qmd
  filter(
    slug == "canada-login-website-en",
    as.Date(date) >= as.Date("2026-01-01"),
    as.Date(date) <= as.Date("2026-06-30"),
    # exclude dates where upstream monitoring was inactive
    response_day_ms > 0
  ) |>
  select(date, uptime_year, uptime_alltime) |>
  arrange(date)

title: Site Uptime
text:
Interpretation notes
The uptime windows are rolling, not calendar-aligned. uptime_month on a given date covers the 30 days trailing that date’s stats update (~23:2x UTC), not a fixed calendar month. To aggregate by calendar month, group by substr(date, 1, 7).
Rolling windows (uptime_week, uptime_month, uptime_year, uptime_alltime) spanning the July 28 – September 23, 2026 gap incorporate unmonitored days recorded as 100% uptime, which may slightly elevate rolling availability figures.

title: Outage Events
text: Individual site outage events detected by the uptime monitor: when a site went down, when it recovered, and the HTTP status code at time of detection.

title: Outage Events
text:
Calculation
Filter sre.uptime_timeseries to rows where status = 'down'. Each such row represents a moment when the upptime bot detected the site was unreachable and committed that state to the history file.
To count outage events per site over a reporting period, group the filtered rows by slug and count.






NoteExample queries






SQLR


All outage events in a reporting period:
SELECT
    date,
    ping_timestamp,
    slug,
    lang,
    http_code,
    response_ms
FROM sre.uptime_timeseries
-- set the reporting window; see the timespans note in cookbook/notes.qmd
WHERE status = 'down'
  AND CAST(date AS DATE) BETWEEN DATE '2026-01-01' AND DATE '2026-06-30'
ORDER BY date DESC, slug;
Outage event count per site in a reporting period:
SELECT
    slug,
    lang,
    COUNT(*) AS outage_event_count
FROM sre.uptime_timeseries
-- set the reporting window; see the timespans note in cookbook/notes.qmd
WHERE status = 'down'
  AND CAST(date AS DATE) BETWEEN DATE '2026-01-01' AND DATE '2026-06-30'
GROUP BY slug, lang
ORDER BY outage_event_count DESC;


All outage events in a reporting period:
tbl(con, in_schema("sre", "uptime_timeseries")) |>
  # set the reporting window; see the timespans note in cookbook/notes.qmd
  filter(
    status == "down",
    as.Date(date) >= as.Date("2026-01-01"),
    as.Date(date) <= as.Date("2026-06-30")
  ) |>
  select(date, ping_timestamp, slug, lang, http_code, response_ms) |>
  arrange(desc(date), slug)
Outage event count per site in a reporting period:
tbl(con, in_schema("sre", "uptime_timeseries")) |>
  # set the reporting window; see the timespans note in cookbook/notes.qmd
  filter(
    status == "down",
    as.Date(date) >= as.Date("2026-01-01"),
    as.Date(date) <= as.Date("2026-06-30")
  ) |>
  count(slug, lang, name = "outage_event_count") |>
  arrange(desc(outage_event_count))

title: Outage Events
text:
Interpretation notes
Each row in sre.uptime_timeseries is a single commit by the upptime bot. On a normal all-up day there is one row per site (the daily ~23:2x UTC snapshot). On an outage day there are additional rows (one when the site went down and one when it recovered), so status = 'down' rows count detection events, not total minutes of downtime. For total outage duration, use the daily_minutes_down JSON field in sre.uptime_summary.
During the July 28 – September 23, 2026 upstream monitoring outage, zero ping commits were executed. The absence of status = 'down' rows during that window reflects inactive synthetic monitoring rather than confirmed 100% uptime.

Site Uptime Metrics
Uptime and response-time metrics for the six monitored CanadaLogin sites, in the sre schema. Data comes from the cds-snc/status-statut GitHub repository and is fetched automatically by the uptime-daily-download Lambda at 04:00 ET each day. No manual steps are required.

title: Weekly Ticket Volume
text: The total number of PSOM tickets captured in each Monday snapshot, showing how the number of tickets in the project changes over time.

title: Weekly Ticket Volume
text:
Calculation
Keep only the Monday date partitions and count the rows in each. The snapshot ran weekly on Mondays until 2026-09-28 and daily from 2026-09-29, so filtering to Mondays gives one comparable total per week across the whole history.






NoteExample queries






SQLR


SELECT
    date,
    COUNT(*) AS ticket_count
FROM jira.psom
WHERE day_of_week(CAST(date AS DATE)) = 1
GROUP BY date
ORDER BY date DESC;


tbl(con, in_schema("jira", "psom")) |>
  filter(wday(as.Date(date), week_start = 1) == 1) |>
  count(date, name = "ticket_count") |>
  arrange(desc(date))

title: Weekly Ticket Volume
text:
Interpretation notes
This counts the tickets still in the project on each Monday, not the tickets opened that week or the open backlog. It includes Done and Canceled tickets until they are archived, and it drops when a batch of tickets is archived (from 52 to 25 between 2026-09-14 and 2026-09-21). The first snapshot, 2026-06-30, was a Tuesday, so the filter leaves it out.

title: SLA Time-to-Done Breach Rate
text:
The proportion of PSOM tickets that missed the “Time to done” SLA, based on the latest snapshot.
This metric reflects how well the team is resolving tickets within the agreed timeframe. It measures the whole ticket, including time spent escalated to another team. Only tickets where the SLA clock started are included; tickets with no clock are excluded.

title: SLA Time-to-Done Breach Rate
text:
Calculation
From jira.psom_sla, filter to the most recent date partition, to sla = 'time_to_done', and to rows where breached is not null (i.e., the clock started). Divide the count of rows where breached is true by the total count of those rows.






NoteExample queries






SQLR


SELECT
    COUNT(*) AS total_sla_tickets,
    SUM(CASE WHEN breached THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS breached_count,
    CAST(SUM(CASE WHEN breached THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS DOUBLE)
        / NULLIF(COUNT(*), 0) AS breach_rate
FROM jira.psom_sla
WHERE date = (SELECT MAX(date) FROM jira.psom_sla)
  AND sla = 'time_to_done'
  AND breached IS NOT NULL;


psom_sla <- tbl(con, in_schema("jira", "psom_sla"))
latest_date <- psom_sla |> summarise(d = max(date, na.rm = TRUE)) |> pull(d)

psom_sla |>
  filter(
    as.Date(date) == as.Date(latest_date),
    sla == "time_to_done",
    !is.na(breached)
  ) |>
  summarise(
    total_sla_tickets = n(),
    breached_count    = sum(as.integer(breached), na.rm = TRUE),
    breach_rate       = sum(as.integer(breached), na.rm = TRUE) / as.double(n())
  )

title: SLA Time-to-Done Breach Rate
text:
Interpretation notes
The rate is a proportion between 0 and 1. Tickets whose clock never started (null breached) are excluded from both numerator and denominator. Check total_sla_tickets to understand the sample size underlying the rate.
The goal is set per ticket (16, 24, 40 and 72 working hours all occur), so a breach means the ticket missed its own target, not a shared one. Working hours run 09:00 to 17:00, so a 40-hour goal is one working week. To compare how long tickets took, use elapsed_minutes instead, which is populated from 2026-09-29.
A ticket that is still open and inside its goal is recorded as not breached (false), the same as a ticket that met the SLA. The rate on a live snapshot is therefore a lower bound: some of those open tickets may still breach before they are resolved. It is most meaningful once the snapshot’s tickets are largely resolved.

title: SLA First-Response Breach Rate
text:
The proportion of PSOM tickets that missed the “Time to first response” SLA, based on the latest snapshot.
This metric is useful for monitoring whether the team is meeting initial response commitments. Only tickets where the SLA clock started are included; tickets with no clock (e.g., non-service-request issue types or tickets created before the SLA scheme was configured) are excluded.

title: About
text:
Conventions
All example SQL targets Amazon Athena (Trino dialect). Constructs such as DATE '...' literals, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (...), and REGEXP_REPLACE follow Trino semantics.
In reporting language, prefer sign-in over login. The underlying IBM Verify field may be called total_logins, but “sign-ins” is preferred (and often enforced) when talking about CanadaLogin.
Where applicable, internal applications are excluded from external-facing adoption reporting. The exclusion list is not maintained here: it is derived from rp.service.is_internal at query time. See the internal applications note in notes.qmd for the pattern.

title: About
text:
Scope
This cookbook covers calculated metrics. Metrics already present in a table without any calculation do not need to be included, although they can be if they need clarification.
The initial version focuses on:

IBM Verify application sign-in metrics
call centre activity metrics

Cross-source metrics comparing sign-in activity and call volume are planned for a future revision.

title: Sign-Ins per Active User (Estimated)
text:
How often a typical user signs in to CanadaLogin over a calendar month, counting only the users who signed in at all that month.
This builds on Completed Sign-In Sessions and inherits its estimate and its assumptions. The denominator is mtd_unique_users read on the month’s last day, so the reporting window has to be whole calendar months.

title: Sign-Ins per Active User (Estimated)
text:
Calculation
Per calendar month, estimate sessions as in Completed Sign-In Sessions: sum successful_logins and subtract the successes of the factors that can complete a sign-in (sms_otp, voice_otp, fido2). Divide by mtd_unique_users on the month’s last day, which is that month’s distinct signed-in users.






NoteExample queries






SQLR


WITH first_factor AS (
    SELECT
        date_trunc('month', from_date) AS month,
        SUM(successful_logins) AS successful_events
    FROM ibm_verify.auth_total_logins
    -- set the reporting window; whole calendar months only
    WHERE from_date BETWEEN DATE '2026-05-01' AND DATE '2026-08-31'
    GROUP BY 1
),

second_factor AS (
    SELECT
        date_trunc('month', from_date) AS month,
        SUM(count) AS mfa_successes
    FROM ibm_verify.mfa_activity
    -- set the reporting window; whole calendar months only
    WHERE from_date BETWEEN DATE '2026-05-01' AND DATE '2026-08-31'
      -- outcome events only; a "sent" OTP is an issuance, not a success
      AND result = 'success'
      -- email_otp validates an email address at sign-up and never enters
      -- successful_logins, so subtracting it would over-correct
      AND mfa_type IN ('sms_otp', 'voice_otp', 'fido2')
    GROUP BY 1
),

active_users AS (
    SELECT month, mtd_unique_users AS monthly_active_users
    FROM (
        SELECT
            date_trunc('month', from_date) AS month,
            mtd_unique_users,
            ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
                PARTITION BY date_trunc('month', from_date)
                ORDER BY from_date DESC
            ) AS day_rank
        FROM ibm_verify.auth_total_logins
        -- set the reporting window; whole calendar months only
        WHERE from_date BETWEEN DATE '2026-05-01' AND DATE '2026-08-31'
    )
    -- mtd_unique_users accumulates through the month, so the last day holds
    -- the month's distinct signed-in users
    WHERE day_rank = 1
)

SELECT
    first_factor.month,
    first_factor.successful_events - second_factor.mfa_successes
        AS estimated_sessions,
    active_users.monthly_active_users,
    CAST(
        first_factor.successful_events - second_factor.mfa_successes AS DOUBLE
    ) / NULLIF(active_users.monthly_active_users, 0)
        AS sign_ins_per_active_user
FROM first_factor
JOIN second_factor ON first_factor.month = second_factor.month
JOIN active_users ON first_factor.month = active_users.month
ORDER BY first_factor.month;


sign_in_types <- c("sms_otp", "voice_otp", "fido2")

first_factor <- tbl(con, in_schema("ibm_verify", "auth_total_logins")) |>
  # set the reporting window; whole calendar months only
  filter(
    from_date >= as.Date("2026-05-01"),
    from_date <= as.Date("2026-08-31")
  ) |>
  group_by(month = floor_date(from_date, "month")) |>
  summarise(successful_events = sum(as.double(successful_logins), na.rm = TRUE))

second_factor <- tbl(con, in_schema("ibm_verify", "mfa_activity")) |>
  # set the reporting window; whole calendar months only
  filter(
    from_date >= as.Date("2026-05-01"),
    from_date <= as.Date("2026-08-31"),
    # outcome events only; a "sent" OTP is an issuance, not a success
    result == "success",
    # email_otp validates an email address at sign-up and never enters
    # successful_logins, so subtracting it would over-correct
    mfa_type %in% sign_in_types
  ) |>
  group_by(month = floor_date(from_date, "month")) |>
  summarise(mfa_successes = sum(as.double(count), na.rm = TRUE))

active_users <- tbl(con, in_schema("ibm_verify", "auth_total_logins")) |>
  # set the reporting window; whole calendar months only
  filter(
    from_date >= as.Date("2026-05-01"),
    from_date <= as.Date("2026-08-31")
  ) |>
  group_by(month = floor_date(from_date, "month")) |>
  # mtd_unique_users accumulates through the month, so the last day holds
  # the month's distinct signed-in users
  filter(from_date == max(from_date, na.rm = TRUE)) |>
  ungroup() |>
  select(month, monthly_active_users = mtd_unique_users)

first_factor |>
  inner_join(second_factor, by = "month") |>
  inner_join(active_users, by = "month") |>
  mutate(
    estimated_sessions = successful_events - mfa_successes,
    sign_ins_per_active_user =
      as.double(estimated_sessions) / as.double(monthly_active_users)
  ) |>
  select(month, estimated_sessions, monthly_active_users, sign_ins_per_active_user) |>
  arrange(month)

title: Authentication Success Rate
text:
The proportion of authentication attempts that succeeded, across all of CanadaLogin. A failed attempt can be a wrong password or a failed second factor.
This metric is useful for monitoring overall authentication health. A sustained drop can indicate a service problem, a misconfigured application, or elevated attack traffic inflating the failure count.

title: Authentication Success Rate
text:
Calculation
Divide the sum of successful_logins by the sum of all attempts (successful_logins + failed_logins) over the selected reporting period.
To track the metric over time, bin the same calculation by week. Truncating from_date to the week groups each day into its Monday-anchored bin, so the result is one success rate per Monday-to-Sunday week.






NoteExample queries






SQLR


Overall:
SELECT
    CAST(SUM(successful_logins) AS DOUBLE)
        / NULLIF(SUM(successful_logins + failed_logins), 0) AS authentication_success_rate
FROM ibm_verify.auth_total_logins
-- set the reporting window; see the timespans note in cookbook/notes.qmd
WHERE from_date BETWEEN DATE '2026-01-01' AND DATE '2026-05-28';
By week:
SELECT
    date_trunc('week', from_date) AS week_start,
    CAST(SUM(successful_logins) AS DOUBLE)
        / NULLIF(SUM(successful_logins + failed_logins), 0) AS authentication_success_rate
FROM ibm_verify.auth_total_logins
-- set the reporting window; see the timespans note in cookbook/notes.qmd
WHERE from_date BETWEEN DATE '2026-01-01' AND DATE '2026-05-28'
-- date_trunc('week', ...) anchors each bin to its Monday
GROUP BY date_trunc('week', from_date)
ORDER BY week_start;


Overall:
tbl(con, in_schema("ibm_verify", "auth_total_logins")) |>
  # set the reporting window; see the timespans note in cookbook/notes.qmd
  filter(
    from_date >= as.Date("2026-01-01"),
    from_date <= as.Date("2026-05-28")
  ) |>
  summarise(
    authentication_success_rate =
      sum(as.double(successful_logins), na.rm = TRUE) /
        sum(successful_logins + failed_logins, na.rm = TRUE)
  )
By week:
tbl(con, in_schema("ibm_verify", "auth_total_logins")) |>
  # set the reporting window; see the timespans note in cookbook/notes.qmd
  filter(
    from_date >= as.Date("2026-01-01"),
    from_date <= as.Date("2026-05-28")
  ) |>
  # floor_date(..., "week") translates to Athena's date_trunc('week', ...),
  # which anchors each bin to its Monday
  mutate(week_start = floor_date(from_date, "week")) |>
  group_by(week_start) |>
  summarise(
    authentication_success_rate =
      sum(as.double(successful_logins), na.rm = TRUE) /
        sum(successful_logins + failed_logins, na.rm = TRUE)
  ) |>

title: Authentication Success Rate
text:
Interpretation notes
The rate is a proportion between 0 and 1. Read it alongside authentication event volume: a low success rate on very low volume may just be noise, while the same rate on high volume is a real signal. In the weekly view, the first and last weeks of the reporting window are usually partial (the window rarely starts or ends on a Monday), so treat boundary weeks with caution when comparing trends.
This rate is computed over authentication methods, not sessions. When signing in to CanadaLogin, IBM Verify records each method as its own event, so a mistyped password is a failed event even when the user then succeeds and completes the sign-in (see the auth_total_logins caveat). The figure measures how often individual authentication steps succeed, not how often a sign-in ultimately completes. The per-application rate counts a different IBM Verify event type, the handoff to a relying party with no factors entered, so the two rates are not comparable.

title: Sign-in MFA Activity by Factor
text:
The volume of MFA attempts across the factors the public can use to sign in, with each factor’s share of the total.
Where All MFA Activity by Factor covers every factor type the platform records, this metric keeps only the ones a member of the public can present as a second factor when signing in: sms_otp, voice_otp, and, since passkeys became generally available on 2026-07-06, fido2. The internal and administrative factors that dominate the platform-wide view are left out.
IBM Verify files MFA as a subtype of the authentication event rather than as an event type of its own, so these counts are a slice of the CanadaLogin-wide authentication events, not an independent stream.
Two factors that reach the public are deliberately excluded:

title: Sign-in MFA Activity by Factor
text:
Calculation
Restrict to the sign-in factors (sms_otp, voice_otp, fido2), then, as in All MFA Activity by Factor, de-duplicate before counting: the OTP factors (sms_otp, voice_otp) record both a sent event and a subsequent success/failure event for the same challenge, so only the sent row is counted for these; fido2 (passkeys) has no sent event and is counted through its success/failure rows. Sum count grouped by mfa_type, then divide each factor’s total by the combined total to get its share.






NoteExample queries






SQLR


SELECT
    mfa_type,
    SUM(count) AS mfa_authentications,
    CAST(SUM(count) AS DOUBLE)
        / NULLIF(SUM(SUM(count)) OVER (), 0) AS factor_share
FROM ibm_verify.mfa_activity
-- set the reporting window; see the timespans note in cookbook/notes.qmd
WHERE from_date BETWEEN DATE '2026-01-01' AND DATE '2026-05-28'
  -- restrict to the factors the public can use to sign in. email_otp is
  -- excluded because it only validates emails at sign-up, and kq, totp, qr,
  -- and ibm_verify_push are internal factors, not public sign-in options.
  AND mfa_type IN ('sms_otp', 'voice_otp', 'fido2')
  -- de-duplicate OTP challenges: count only "sent" for the OTP factors
  -- (sms_otp, voice_otp), and "success"/"failure" for fido2 (passkeys),
  -- which has no "sent" event.
  AND (
    result = 'sent'
    OR (
      result IN ('success', 'failure')
      AND mfa_type NOT IN ('sms_otp', 'email_otp', 'voice_otp')
    )
  )
GROUP BY mfa_type
ORDER BY mfa_authentications DESC;


otp_types <- c("sms_otp", "email_otp", "voice_otp")
sign_in_types <- c("sms_otp", "voice_otp", "fido2")

tbl(con, in_schema("ibm_verify", "mfa_activity")) |>
  # set the reporting window; see the timespans note in cookbook/notes.qmd
  filter(
    from_date >= as.Date("2026-01-01"),
    from_date <= as.Date("2026-05-28"),
    # restrict to the factors the public can use to sign in. email_otp is
    # excluded because it only validates emails at sign-up, and kq, totp, qr,
    # and ibm_verify_push are internal factors, not public sign-in options.
    mfa_type %in% sign_in_types,
    # de-duplicate OTP challenges: count only "sent" for the OTP factors
    # (sms_otp, voice_otp), and "success"/"failure" for fido2 (passkeys),
    # which has no "sent" event.
    result == "sent" |
      (result %in% c("success", "failure") & !mfa_type %in% otp_types)
  ) |>
  group_by(mfa_type) |>
  summarise(
    mfa_authentications = sum(count, na.rm = TRUE)
  ) |>
  mutate(
    factor_share =
      as.double(mfa_authentications) / sum(mfa_authentications, na.rm = TRUE)
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(mfa_authentications))

Passkey (fido2) activity appears only from the 2026-07-06 rollout onward, so a reporting window that predates that date will show little or none.

title: MFA Success Rate
text:
The proportion of MFA attempts that succeeded over a selected reporting period.
This metric is useful for monitoring how often users clear the second factor. A falling rate can point to user friction with a particular factor, delivery problems (for example, undelivered SMS or email OTPs), or attack traffic.

title: MFA Success Rate
text:
Calculation
Divide the sum of count where result = 'success' by the sum of count where result is 'success' or 'failure'. OTP factor types also produce a 'sent' event per challenge, which must be excluded from both the numerator and the denominator, because sent rows do not represent outcomes.
To track the metric over time, bin the same calculation by week. Truncating from_date to the week groups each day into its Monday-anchored bin, so the result is one success rate per Monday-to-Sunday week.






NoteExample queries






SQLR


Overall:
SELECT
    CAST(SUM(count) FILTER (WHERE result = 'success') AS DOUBLE)
        / NULLIF(SUM(count), 0) AS mfa_success_rate
FROM ibm_verify.mfa_activity
-- set the reporting window; see the timespans note in cookbook/notes.qmd
WHERE from_date BETWEEN DATE '2026-01-01' AND DATE '2026-05-28'
  -- exclude "sent" rows; success rate is calculated from outcome events only.
  -- including "sent" would inflate the denominator and deflate the rate.
  AND result IN ('success', 'failure');
By week:
SELECT
    date_trunc('week', from_date) AS week_start,
    CAST(SUM(count) FILTER (WHERE result = 'success') AS DOUBLE)
        / NULLIF(SUM(count), 0) AS mfa_success_rate
FROM ibm_verify.mfa_activity
-- set the reporting window; see the timespans note in cookbook/notes.qmd
WHERE from_date BETWEEN DATE '2026-01-01' AND DATE '2026-05-28'
  -- exclude "sent" rows; success rate is calculated from outcome events only.
  -- including "sent" would inflate the denominator and deflate the rate.
  AND result IN ('success', 'failure')
-- date_trunc('week', ...) anchors each bin to its Monday
GROUP BY date_trunc('week', from_date)
ORDER BY week_start;

    # including "sent" would inflate the denominator and deflate the rate.

title: MFA Authentications
text:
The total number of MFA attempts over a selected reporting period.
This metric measures second-factor authentication volume. It counts attempts, not people, and includes both successful and failed challenges.

title: MFA Authentications
text:
Calculation
Sum count over the selected reporting period. OTP factor types (sms_otp, email_otp, voice_otp) record both a sent event and a subsequent success/failure event for the same challenge; to avoid double-counting, only the sent row is used for these types. Non-OTP factor types (fido2, kq, totp, ibm_verify_push) do not generate a sent event, so their success/failure rows are used instead. Add a result breakdown to separate successes from failures.






NoteExample queries






SQLR


SELECT
    SUM(count) AS mfa_authentications
FROM ibm_verify.mfa_activity
-- set the reporting window; see the timespans note in cookbook/notes.qmd
WHERE from_date BETWEEN DATE '2026-01-01' AND DATE '2026-05-28'
  -- OTP types record both a "sent" event and a "success"/"failure" event for
  -- the same challenge. Counting all three would double-count these attempts.
  -- Non-OTP types (fido2, kq, totp, ibm_verify_push) have no "sent" event
  -- and must be counted through their "success"/"failure" rows instead.
  AND (
    result = 'sent'
    OR (
      result IN ('success', 'failure')
      AND mfa_type NOT IN ('sms_otp', 'email_otp', 'voice_otp')
    )
  );


otp_types <- c("sms_otp", "email_otp", "voice_otp")

  filter(
    from_date >= as.Date("2026-01-01"),
    from_date <= as.Date("2026-05-28"),
    # OTP types record both a "sent" and a "success"/"failure" event per
    # challenge; use only "sent" for these to avoid double-counting.
    # Non-OTP types have no "sent" event, so use "success"/"failure".
    result == "sent" |
      (result %in% c("success", "failure") & !mfa_type %in% otp_types)
  ) |>
  summarise(
    mfa_authentications = sum(count, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

title: Cumulative Unique Users
text:
The total number of distinct users who have signed in to CanadaLogin over a chosen reporting window: this month or this calendar year.
This metric is useful for understanding the overall reach and adoption of CanadaLogin over time. Note that it will not align with the sum of unique users across individual apps: a user who signs into App A and App B on the same day counts as two unique users at the app level but only one overall.

title: Cumulative Unique Users
text:
Calculation
Take the latest value of the cumulative unique-user column for the window of interest. The window is chosen by which column you read, not by a date filter (see the note on reporting timespans):

mtd_unique_users for month-to-date
ytd_unique_users for year-to-date

These columns are cumulative, so the most recent row holds the current total.






Warning



ytd_unique_users may be unreliable. IBM Verify computes it over a longer window than its underlying data retention actually covers, so the figure can undercount and has been seen decreasing from one day to the next. Treat it as an estimate only, and prefer mtd_unique_users where the reporting question allows. See Why Unique Users Cannot Be Added Up for detail.


A since_apr22_unique_users column (cumulative distinct users since launch) was previously available but has been removed; see the data retention note.






NoteExample queries






SQLR


Month-to-date:
SELECT
    mtd_unique_users
FROM ibm_verify.auth_total_logins
ORDER BY from_date DESC
LIMIT 1;
Year-to-date:
SELECT
    ytd_unique_users
FROM ibm_verify.auth_total_logins
ORDER BY from_date DESC
LIMIT 1;


Month-to-date:
tbl(con, in_schema("ibm_verify", "auth_total_logins")) |>
  slice_max(
    from_date,
    n = 1,
    with_ties = FALSE
  ) |>
  pull(mtd_unique_users)
Year-to-date:
tbl(con, in_schema("ibm_verify", "auth_total_logins")) |>
  slice_max(
    from_date,
    n = 1,
    with_ties = FALSE
  ) |>
  pull(ytd_unique_users)

title: Cumulative Unique Users
text:
Interpretation notes
Each column resets on its own cadence: mtd_unique_users resets at the start of each month and ytd_unique_users at the start of each calendar year. Do not sum these columns across rows; they are already cumulative.

title: Completed Sign-In Sessions (Estimated)
text: An estimate of the number of completed sign-in sessions to CanadaLogin over a selected reporting period, where a session is one user getting all the way through the sign-in flow regardless of how many authentication methods it took.

title: Completed Sign-In Sessions (Estimated)
text:
Calculation
A completed session has exactly one successful first-factor event (the password) plus zero or more successful second factors. Both kinds of success are lumped together in successful_logins on auth_total_logins, while the second-factor successes are counted separately on mfa_activity. Subtracting the second from the first leaves one event per session: the first-factor success. So sum successful_logins over the window and subtract the sum of mfa_activity.count where result = 'success', restricted to the factors that can complete a sign-in.






NoteExample queries






SQLR


WITH first_factor AS (
    SELECT SUM(successful_logins) AS successful_events
    FROM ibm_verify.auth_total_logins
    -- set the reporting window; see the timespans note in cookbook/notes.qmd
    WHERE from_date BETWEEN DATE '2026-01-01' AND DATE '2026-05-28'
),

second_factor AS (
    SELECT SUM(count) AS mfa_successes
    FROM ibm_verify.mfa_activity
    -- set the reporting window; see the timespans note in cookbook/notes.qmd
    WHERE from_date BETWEEN DATE '2026-01-01' AND DATE '2026-05-28'
      -- outcome events only; a "sent" OTP is an issuance, not a success
      AND result = 'success'
      -- email_otp validates an email address at sign-up and never enters
      -- successful_logins, so subtracting it would over-correct
      AND mfa_type IN ('sms_otp', 'voice_otp', 'fido2')
)

SELECT
    first_factor.successful_events - second_factor.mfa_successes
        AS estimated_completed_sessions
FROM first_factor
CROSS JOIN second_factor;


sign_in_types <- c("sms_otp", "voice_otp", "fido2")

successful_events <- tbl(con, in_schema("ibm_verify", "auth_total_logins")) |>
  # set the reporting window; see the timespans note in cookbook/notes.qmd
  filter(
    from_date >= as.Date("2026-01-01"),
    from_date <= as.Date("2026-05-28")
  ) |>
  summarise(successful_events = sum(as.double(successful_logins), na.rm = TRUE)) |>
  pull(successful_events)

mfa_successes <- tbl(con, in_schema("ibm_verify", "mfa_activity")) |>
  # set the reporting window; see the timespans note in cookbook/notes.qmd
  filter(
    from_date >= as.Date("2026-01-01"),
    from_date <= as.Date("2026-05-28"),
    # outcome events only; a "sent" OTP is an issuance, not a success
    result == "success",
    # email_otp validates an email address at sign-up and never enters
    # successful_logins, so subtracting it would over-correct
    mfa_type %in% sign_in_types
  ) |>
  summarise(mfa_successes = sum(as.double(count), na.rm = TRUE)) |>
  pull(mfa_successes)

successful_events - mfa_successes

text:
Interpretation notes
The estimate works because each session contributes exactly one first-factor success no matter how many second factors it used:









Session type
successful_logins

email_otp is excluded because a successful email_otp does not increment successful_logins. It validates an email address at sign-up rather than completing a sign-in.
The estimate rests on two assumptions:

Passwordless and FIDO-first logins are undercounted. A session whose only factor is FIDO2 is one event in successful_logins and also a fido2 success in mfa_activity, so it nets to zero. The figure is therefore a slight underestimate.
The two tables are assumed to count sign-in second-factor successes the same way. Both derive from the same IBM Verify event stream, which makes this plausible, but it is not guaranteed by anything in the data catalog.

Because of these assumptions, label the result as estimated wherever it is reported, and never present it as an exact session count. When the question is about distinct people rather than sessions, prefer unique_users (daily active users), which needs no assumptions: a user cannot be a unique user without completing a sign-in.

title: Applications per Credential
text:
The average number of distinct applications a single credential reaches.
This metric measures how far the typical user spreads across CanadaLogin-integrated applications. It works because per-application unique_users counts each person once per application, while the CanadaLogin-wide count counts each person once overall: a user active on three applications adds three to the per-application sum but only one to the overall total. Dividing the two recovers the average number of applications per credential.
A value of 1.0 means the typical credential touches exactly one application; 2.0 means two, and so on.

title: Applications per Credential
text:
Calculation
Sum the latest year-to-date unique users across every application (from app_login_counts), then divide by the latest CanadaLogin-wide year-to-date unique users (from auth_total_logins). Both inputs are cumulative ytd_unique_users fields, so take the latest value per source rather than summing across days.






Warning



This metric’s default calculation relies on ytd_unique_users, which may be unreliable: IBM Verify computes it over a longer window than its underlying data retention actually covers, so the figure can undercount. Treat the result as an estimate only, or swap in mtd_unique_users on both sides for a more reliable month-to-date figure (see below). See Why Unique Users Cannot Be Added Up for detail.








NoteExample queries






SQLR


WITH app_latest AS (
    SELECT
        application_name,
        ytd_unique_users,
        ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
            PARTITION BY application_name
            ORDER BY from_date DESC
        ) AS rn
    FROM ibm_verify.app_login_counts
),

app_total AS (
    SELECT SUM(ytd_unique_users) AS sum_app_unique_users
    FROM app_latest
    WHERE rn = 1
),

overall_total AS (
    SELECT ytd_unique_users AS overall_unique_users
    FROM ibm_verify.auth_total_logins
    ORDER BY from_date DESC
    LIMIT 1
)

SELECT
    CAST(app_total.sum_app_unique_users AS DOUBLE)
        / NULLIF(overall_total.overall_unique_users, 0) AS applications_per_credential
FROM app_total
CROSS JOIN overall_total;


sum_app_unique_users <- tbl(con, in_schema("ibm_verify", "app_login_counts")) |>
  group_by(application_name) |>
  slice_max(
    from_date,
    n = 1,
    with_ties = FALSE
  ) |>
  ungroup() |>
  summarise(
    sum_app_unique_users = sum(as.double(ytd_unique_users), na.rm = TRUE)
  ) |>
  pull(sum_app_unique_users)

overall_unique_users <- tbl(con, in_schema("ibm_verify", "auth_total_logins")) |>
  slice_max(
    from_date,
    n = 1,
    with_ties = FALSE
  ) |>
  pull(ytd_unique_users)

sum_app_unique_users / overall_unique_users

title: Applications per Credential
text:
Interpretation notes
This is a population average, not a per-user count: a small group of power users spanning many applications can pull it up while most credentials stay on one.
The figure is inflated by internal applications, especially the migration app (GCS Migration Solution) and the profile management app (GC Sign In - Profile Management App). A user who reaches a single public service is still recorded as a unique user in the migration app when their credential is migrated from ECM, and in the profile management app when they manage their account, so they count two or three times in the per-application sum while counting once overall. To measure breadth across public-facing services, exclude the internal applications (listed at the top of this chapter) from the per-application sum.
Swap ytd_unique_users for mtd_unique_users to measure the same breadth over a different window.

title: Task Success Rate
text:
The proportion of users who started a given task in CanadaLogin and reached that task’s defined end point, measured from Google Analytics 4 funnel data.
This is a family of metrics, not a single number. Each funnel declares its own task success rate as a step_ratio in its YAML definition on GitHub. The entry and exit steps for each funnel are described below as of this writing, but the YAML is the canonical, versioned source - see funnel_src/funnels/ in the canadalogin-reporting-data-pipeline repo.
Only sign-up, password recovery and the two migration tasks end on a screen that confirms the task is done. Sign-in cannot, and the 2-step recovery exit is a later cleanup screen. See the task notes before comparing tasks or reading any one rate as a completion rate.

title: Task Success Rate
text:
Calculation
Each funnel’s task success rate is already computed and stored as one row per window in funnel_metrics: the exit step’s activeUsers divided by the entry step’s, for that funnel run. There is no ratio to compute by hand - filter to the funnel and metric, and read value. Query funnel_metrics_current rather than funnel_metrics directly, so a future funnel version bump can’t silently blend two definitions together. Filter breakdown_value = 'RESERVED_TOTAL' for the overall rate across all relying parties; substitute a specific relying party name for a per-RP figure. The funnels catalog entry explains the RESERVED_TOTAL and window_incomplete conventions.
For one task, set funnel_id to the value given in that task’s notes.






NoteExample queries






SQLR


One task:
SELECT
    window_end,
    value AS task_success_rate
FROM google_analytics.funnel_metrics_current
WHERE funnel_id = 'sign_in'
  AND metric_id = 'task_success'
  AND window_days = '7'
  AND breakdown_value = 'RESERVED_TOTAL'
  AND NOT window_incomplete
  -- set the reporting window; see the timespans note in cookbook/notes.qmd
  AND CAST(window_end AS DATE) BETWEEN DATE '2026-07-14' AND DATE '2026-08-03'
ORDER BY window_end;
Every task:
SELECT
    funnel_id,
    window_end,
    value AS task_success_rate
FROM google_analytics.funnel_metrics_current
WHERE metric_id = 'task_success'
  AND window_days = '7'
  AND breakdown_value = 'RESERVED_TOTAL'
  AND NOT window_incomplete
  -- set the reporting window; see the timespans note in cookbook/notes.qmd
  AND CAST(window_end AS DATE) BETWEEN DATE '2026-08-03' AND DATE '2026-08-31'
ORDER BY funnel_id, window_end;


One task:
tbl(con, in_schema("google_analytics", "funnel_metrics_current")) |>
  filter(
    funnel_id == "sign_in",
    metric_id == "task_success",
    window_days == "7",
    breakdown_value == "RESERVED_TOTAL",
    !window_incomplete,
    # set the reporting window; see the timespans note in cookbook/notes.qmd
    as.Date(window_end) >= as.Date("2026-07-14"),
    as.Date(window_end) <= as.Date("2026-08-03")
  ) |>
  select(window_end, task_success_rate = value) |>
  arrange(window_end)
Every task:
tbl(con, in_schema("google_analytics", "funnel_metrics_current")) |>
  filter(
    metric_id == "task_success",
    window_days == "7",
    breakdown_value == "RESERVED_TOTAL",
    !window_incomplete,
    # set the reporting window; see the timespans note in cookbook/notes.qmd
    as.Date(window_end) >= as.Date("2026-08-03"),
    as.Date(window_end) <= as.Date("2026-08-31")
  ) |>
  select(funnel_id, window_end, task_success_rate = value) |>
  arrange(funnel_id, window_end)

title: Task Success Rate
text:
Interpretation notes
The queries above use window_days = '7', a rolling weekly rate recomputed nightly on a 7-day window ending each date. Three window lengths exist, and switching between them is a one-line change:

'1' is the same metric on a single day. It is the noisiest of the three, but it is the only one that shows the exact date something changed.
'7' is the usual default. Every window holds one of each weekday, so day-of-week effects wash out.
'28' is a rolling four-week window. It is the steadiest of the three and the one to use for monthly reporting.

Windows overlap, so consecutive rows are not independent. One unusual day shows up in 7 weekly rows and 28 monthly ones. A NULL rate means nobody reached the entry step in that window. These rows are rare. Drop them rather than counting them as 0.0, or an average will read too low.

Task notes

All tasks

Users, not attempts. Every step counts distinct activeUsers in the window. A user who fails, retries and succeeds counts once, as a success. A user who fails three times and gives up counts once, as a failure. The rate is a share of people, not of attempts.
Sign ups and sign ins without a valid destination RP are excluded. It is technically possible for someone to go through the sign up or sign in flow without entering via a valid RP service, via a link that specifies the CL manage app as the destination relying party. Actual users will always enter via a valid RP, so we can be confident that traffic with the Manage CanadaLogin RP id parameter represents internal employee traffic, rather than actul users. All funnels that are not manage app tasks therefore exclude traffic with the Manage App RP id parameter. Manage CanadaLogin app, which is internal. See Internal applications.
A series can change definition part way through. funnel_metrics_current returns the newest version for each date, and a new version is not always backfilled. Check funnel_version across the rows before reading a trend.



Sign in

Funnel ID: sign_in
Definition: sign_in.yaml
Entry: enter_email, the “Enter your email” screen
Exit: mfa_submit, pressing submit on the second-factor form

This rate measures submitting a second factor, but not necessarily success. The exit is pressing the submit button on the second-factor form. It is possible to submit an incorrect OTP code and count as a success in the task but fail to actually sign in. This is a limitation of what Google Analytics measures. This means the rate is marginally overstated, compared to a true sign-in success rate.
For an authentication success rate measured by IBM Verify itself, see Authentication Success Rate. It counts attempts rather than users and covers every sign-in, not only those that started in a tagged browser session, so the two numbers will not match.


Sign up

Funnel ID: sign_up
Definition: sign_up.yaml
Entry: terms, the Terms and Conditions screen
Exit: complete, the “Your CanadaLogin is complete” screen



Recover password

Funnel ID: recover_password
Definition: recover_password.yaml
Entry: reset_password, the “Reset your password” screen
Exit: complete, the “Your password has been reset” screen

Many people who start are checking whether they have an account. They enter their email, enter the OTP code sent to them, and get error 26 (“This email is not associated with an account”). The funnel counts them as failures. Resolving this issue is a work in progress.


Recover 2-step verification

Funnel ID: recover_2sv
Definition: recover_2sv.yaml
Entry: initiate_recovery, the “Initiate email verification” screen
Exit: confirmation, the “Delete sign-in methods you’re not using anymore” screen
Exit is a cleanup screen, not a confirmation. The last step is “Delete sign-in methods you’re not using anymore”, offered after a new method is set up.



Migration
Existing account:

Funnel ID: migration_existing_to_cl
Definition: migration_existing_to_cl.yaml
Entry: migration_not_skipped, answering the legacy sign-in prompt without skipping
Exit: migration_complete, the “Migration - Confirmation” screen

New account:

Funnel ID: migration_new_to_cl
Definition: migration_new_to_cl.yaml
Entry: migration_not_skipped, answering the legacy sign-in prompt without skipping
Exit: migration_complete, the “Migration - Confirmation” screen
The denominator is not the first step. In both funnels, task_success divides by migration_not_skipped, users who answered the legacy sign-in prompt without skipping it. The rate is the share of people who chose to link a legacy method and finished.
The prompt step has a time limit in migration_existing_to_cl. The legacy method prompt must follow the 2-step verification step within 30 minutes.

title: Top 10 Call Topics
text:
The ten most common call topics in the call centre topic data.
This is useful for quickly identifying the most common reasons people contact the call centre.

title: Top 10 Call Topics
text:
Calculation
Count records by cleaned topic, calculate topic share, and return the top 10 by topic count.






NoteExample queries






SQLR


WITH topic_counts AS (
    SELECT
        REGEXP_REPLACE(TRIM(statobject), '\s+', ' ') AS call_topic,
        COUNT(*) AS topic_count
    FROM call_centre.weekly_topic_dump
    GROUP BY REGEXP_REPLACE(TRIM(statobject), '\s+', ' ')
),

topic_shares AS (
    SELECT
        call_topic,
        topic_count,
        CAST(topic_count AS DOUBLE)
            / NULLIF(SUM(topic_count) OVER (), 0) AS topic_share
    FROM topic_counts
)

SELECT
    call_topic,
    topic_count,
    topic_share
FROM topic_shares
-- sort on topic_count desc, then call_topic asc to break ties deterministically
ORDER BY topic_count DESC, call_topic
LIMIT 10;


tbl(con, in_schema("call_centre", "weekly_topic_dump")) |>
  mutate(
    call_topic = str_squish(statobject)
  ) |>
  count(call_topic, name = "topic_count") |>
  mutate(
    topic_share = as.double(topic_count) / sum(topic_count, na.rm = TRUE)
  ) |>
  # sort on topic_count desc, then call_topic asc to break ties deterministically
  arrange(desc(topic_count), call_topic) |>
  head(10)

title: Calls per Active User
text:
Call centre volume divided by the size of the active user base, so you can compare support demand across weeks even as the user base grows.
Raw call volume moves partly because the number of people using CanadaLogin changes. Normalizing by active users takes that out and leaves how often a typical user needed to phone in on a given day. The figure is scaled to calls per 100 active users to keep it in a readable range.

title: Calls per Active User
text:
Calculation
For each call centre reporting week, take calls_accepted from call_centre.weekly_activity_report, subtract that week’s test_calls, and divide by the total user-days in that week, then multiply by 100. User-days is the sum of ibm_verify.auth_total_logins.unique_users over the days whose date falls inside the week’s date_range_start to date_range_end, so the numerator and the denominator cover the same span of days. A weekly call count over weekly user-days is a per-day rate. The two tables store their dates as text, so both sides of the join are cast to DATE.
Use calls_accepted, not calls_answered: accepted counts everything that reached the queue, so an abandoned call still counts as demand. test_calls is a subset of accepted and is large enough at current volumes to be worth subtracting.






NoteExample queries






SQLR


SELECT
    w.date_range_start,
    w.date_range_end,
    CAST(w.calls_accepted AS BIGINT) AS calls_accepted,
    CAST(COALESCE(w.test_calls, 0) AS BIGINT) AS test_calls,
    CAST(w.calls_accepted - COALESCE(w.test_calls, 0) AS BIGINT) AS calls_excl_test,
    AVG(a.unique_users) AS avg_daily_active_users,
    CAST(w.calls_accepted - COALESCE(w.test_calls, 0) AS DOUBLE)
        / SUM(a.unique_users) * 100 AS calls_per_100_dau
FROM call_centre.weekly_activity_report AS w
JOIN ibm_verify.auth_total_logins AS a
    ON CAST(a.date AS DATE)
       BETWEEN CAST(w.date_range_start AS DATE) AND CAST(w.date_range_end AS DATE)
GROUP BY w.date_range_start, w.date_range_end, w.calls_accepted, w.test_calls
ORDER BY w.date_range_start;


weekly <- tbl(con, in_schema("call_centre", "weekly_activity_report")) |>
  select(date_range_start, date_range_end, calls_accepted, test_calls)

dau <- tbl(con, in_schema("ibm_verify", "auth_total_logins")) |>
  select(dau_date = date, unique_users)

weekly |>
  cross_join(dau) |>
  filter(
    as.Date(dau_date) >= as.Date(date_range_start),
    as.Date(dau_date) <= as.Date(date_range_end)
  ) |>
  group_by(date_range_start, date_range_end, calls_accepted, test_calls) |>
  summarise(
    avg_daily_active_users = mean(unique_users, na.rm = TRUE),
    user_days = sum(unique_users, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    test_calls = coalesce(test_calls, 0),
    calls_excl_test = calls_accepted - test_calls,
    calls_per_100_dau = calls_excl_test / user_days * 100
  ) |>
  arrange(date_range_start) |>
  select(
    date_range_start,
    date_range_end,
    calls_accepted,
    test_calls,
    calls_excl_test,
    avg_daily_active_users,
    calls_per_100_dau
  )

title: Calls per Active User
text:
Interpretation notes
Both sides are per-day averages over the same Sunday to Saturday week: average daily calls over average daily active users. On a typical day, roughly this many calls came in per 100 active users. This converts cleanly to a percentage, e.g., 2 calls per 100 users means 2% of users called on a given day.
Watch the units. Dividing a whole week of calls by one day’s active users reads about seven times too high. Normalizing by user-days avoids that and holds up for a partial week, since the day count comes from the data rather than a hardcoded 7. avg_daily_active_users is output for auditing only; the rate comes from the sum.
A call centre week runs Sunday to Saturday, from the report’s own date_range_start and date_range_end. The IBM Verify metrics anchor weeks on Monday, so the two do not line up; the join and the denominator follow the call centre boundaries.
A week appears only once daily active user data exists for it, so the series starts near the April 22, 2026 launch.

title: Average Handle Time
text:
The average total time agents spend per call, including any after-call wrap-up.
avg_handle_time_seconds covers more than avg_call_length_seconds: it adds wrap-up work after the caller disconnects. Like the other averages, combine weeks with a weighted mean.

title: Average Handle Time
text:
Calculation
Calculate a weighted average of avg_handle_time_seconds, weighted by calls_answered.






NoteExample queries






SQLR


SELECT
    SUM(
        CAST(avg_handle_time_seconds AS DOUBLE)
        * CAST(calls_answered AS DOUBLE)
    )
    / NULLIF(SUM(CAST(calls_answered AS DOUBLE)), 0) AS weighted_avg_handle_time_seconds
FROM call_centre.weekly_activity_report
WHERE CAST(date_range_start AS DATE) BETWEEN DATE '2026-01-01' AND DATE '2026-05-31';


tbl(con, in_schema("call_centre", "weekly_activity_report")) |>
  filter(
    as.Date(date_range_start) >= as.Date("2026-01-01"),
    as.Date(date_range_start) <= as.Date("2026-05-31")
  ) |>
  summarise(
    weighted_avg_handle_time_seconds =
      sum(avg_handle_time_seconds * calls_answered, na.rm = TRUE) /
        sum(calls_answered, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

title: Abandonment Rate
text:
The proportion of accepted calls that were abandoned before being answered.
This metric is useful for understanding how often callers give up while waiting. It is closely tied to wait times: rising delay often drives rising abandonment.

title: Abandonment Rate
text:
Calculation
Divide the sum of calls_abandoned by the sum of calls_accepted over the selected reporting period. Summing the raw counts gives a volume-weighted rate; do not average the weekly calls_abandoned_pct column.






NoteExample queries






SQLR


SELECT
    SUM(CAST(calls_abandoned AS DOUBLE))
        / NULLIF(SUM(CAST(calls_accepted AS DOUBLE)), 0) AS abandonment_rate
FROM call_centre.weekly_activity_report
WHERE CAST(date_range_start AS DATE) BETWEEN DATE '2026-01-01' AND DATE '2026-05-31';


tbl(con, in_schema("call_centre", "weekly_activity_report")) |>
  filter(
    as.Date(date_range_start) >= as.Date("2026-01-01"),
    as.Date(date_range_start) <= as.Date("2026-05-31")
  ) |>
  summarise(
    abandonment_rate =
      sum(calls_abandoned, na.rm = TRUE) /
        sum(calls_accepted, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

Notes
Join on alias alone. Do not filter on source. source records where the name was first seen, not which system the name belongs to. Filtering by it before joining will silently drop matches for any alias that turns up in both systems.
One service, several aliases. A service has as many rows here as it has names. For example, MyCGC is MyCGC in Google Analytics but both MyCGC - CGC - .NET - Prod and MyCGC - CGC - Power Pages - Prod in IBM Verify. Joining a fact table through this lookup is a many-to-one join, so aggregate after the join, not before.
Not every string in the analytics tables is an alias. The rp_name breakdown in the Google Analytics funnel tables also contains RESERVED_TOTAL (the all-services rollup), (not set), and the empty string. None of these are services, and an inner join drops them. If you are reconciling totals, exclude RESERVED_TOTAL explicitly rather than relying on the join to remove it.
Aliases are exact strings, not patterns. They are matched literally, with no trimming or case folding. A new application name in IBM Verify will not resolve until it is added to the source sheet by hand.

title: ibm_verify.mfa_activity
text:
Notes
Only OTP factor types (sms_otp, email_otp, voice_otp) generate a “sent” event, because they are issued before the user responds. Successfully clearing one of these challenges therefore counts as two events: first a “sent” event, then either a “success” or “failure” event depending on how the user responds. It is possible to generate multiple “success”/“failure” events on a single “sent” event if the user inputs their OTP incorrectly first and then correctly. Non-OTP factor types (fido2, kq, totp, ibm_verify_push) have no “sent” event and produce only “success”/“failure” rows.
When calculating MFA usage metrics, de-duplicate accordingly: count “sent” events for OTP factors (sending an email OTP but not using it is still usage), and “success”/“failure” events for non-OTP factors. Summing “sent” alone would silently drop every non-OTP factor.
When calculating success rate metrics, use the number of successful events divided by the sum of the success and failure events, excluding “sent”.

rolling_365d_unique_users is null before 2026-06-13, its implementation date.






Warning



ytd_unique_users and rolling_365d_unique_users may be unreliable. Both are computed by IBM Verify over a longer window than its underlying data retention actually covers, so the figures can undercount, and ytd_unique_users has been seen decreasing from one day to the next. Treat both as estimates only. See Why Unique Users Cannot Be Added Up for detail.


A since_apr22_unique_users field (cumulative distinct users since the April 22, 2026 public launch) was previously provided here. It has been removed from the pipeline because the source API retains only the most recent 366.5 days of data, so a since-launch cumulative count cannot be maintained once launch is more than a year in the past. See the retention note on the IBM Verify catalog overview.
Unlike auth_total_logins, these counts are not inflated by second factors. The per-authentication-method event inflation described there only happens when a person signs in to CanadaLogin itself. Reaching an integrated application uses the session they already hold: CanadaLogin issues the application a freshly minted assertion or token, the person enters no password or second factor, and one handoff records one SSO event. total_logins and successful_logins still count events rather than people, because one person can reach an application repeatedly. Use unique_users when the question is about how many distinct people used the application.

title: google_analytics.funnels_current
text:
A view over funnels that resolves the current funnel_version automatically. Query this instead of funnels directly unless a specific past version is genuinely what’s wanted.

Keywords: Google Analytics, GA4, funnel, funnel version, current version

title: google_analytics.funnels_current
text:
Definition
CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW funnels_current AS
WITH latest_per_date AS (
  SELECT funnel_id, window_days, window_end,
         MAX(CAST(funnel_version AS integer)) AS current_version
  FROM funnels
  GROUP BY funnel_id, window_days, window_end
)
SELECT f.*
FROM funnels f
JOIN latest_per_date d
  ON  f.funnel_id   = d.funnel_id
  AND f.window_days = d.window_days
  AND f.window_end  = d.window_end
  AND CAST(f.funnel_version AS integer) = d.current_version;

title: google_analytics.funnels_current
text:
Notes
The partition keys are still typed string in the view’s output, the same as the base table - MAX(funnel_version) on the view still sorts lexically wrong if you ignore that the view has already picked one version per row. Query it the same way you’d query funnels: filter with quoted string literals (WHERE window_days = '7', not = 7), and don’t re-aggregate across funnel_version since the view has already resolved it.
Resolution is per (funnel_id, window_days, window_end), not a global max per funnel. If a funnel bumps from version 1 to version 2 partway through its history, dates before the bump still resolve to version 1 (version 2 was never run for them) and dates from the bump onward resolve to version 2 - one continuous time series, not a series that vanishes before the bump. This only holds because versions of the same funnel are assumed to measure the same underlying thing; it would not be a safe pattern for two versions that represent genuinely different metrics.

title: Google Analytics
text:
Export lag
All four tables are pulled with a deliberate two-day lag - the nightly sweep that runs the morning of August 5, 2026 lands a window ending August 3, 2026, not August 4, because GA4 takes 24 to 48 hours to finish processing a day’s events. Each day is written once and never re-pulled, so a window read too early would stay artificially low forever.
Two of these tables - funnels and funnel_metrics - are defined by version-controlled YAML rather than a fixed schema. For what a funnel step or a derived metric actually measures, the YAML on GitHub is the single canonical source, not this catalog: steps get renamed, re-scoped, or added as CanadaLogin’s own pages change, and the table pages describe the table shape rather than the current step names. See funnel_src/funnels/ in the pipeline repo.

A metric is recomputed automatically when its funnel’s funnel_version bumps (the same nightly job backfills every past window under the new version), but adding a metrics: block to a funnel for the first time also triggers a one-time backfill across that funnel’s entire already-landed history - so a metric’s earliest window_end is not necessarily the date the metric was defined.

title: google_analytics.funnels
text:
Notes
A funnel’s step names, order and population can change between versions - always check GitHub, not a memory of a prior version. Every CanadaLogin funnel has already had at least one step renamed or re-scoped since it was first defined (see the task success rate metric for a worked example). funnel_version exists so old and new definitions coexist rather than silently overwriting each other: always pin funnel_version in a query, or use the funnels_current view, which resolves the newest version per date automatically. Summing or averaging across versions blends two different definitions of the funnel into one meaningless number.
RESERVED_TOTAL is a real GA4 sentinel, not a relying party. A funnel breakdown caps at 15 distinct values; RESERVED_TOTAL is GA4’s grand total across all relying parties, including any beyond that cap, and is the correct number to read as the funnel’s overall rate.
window_incomplete rows are written, not dropped, and must be excluded from a trend. A window that reaches earlier than a funnel’s valid_from (or later than valid_to) is trimmed and flagged rather than skipped, so a scheduled job keeps running as a tagging boundary recedes.
activeusers is de-duplicated within its own window and is not additive across windows. Summing seven daily (window_days = "1") rows for a week, for example, is not the same query as one window_days = "7" row for that week - repeat users within the week are counted once by the 7-day row and once per day they appeared by the daily rows. Never sum activeusers across rows with different window_end or window_days values.

title: IBM Verify
text:
Data retention
The dataset behind the IBM Verify reporting API retains only the most recent 366.5 days of data. This does not limit the tables here. The daily aggregate rows are stored on our side and kept beyond a year, so any metric we calculate by aggregating those stored daily rows (authentication events, SSO events, MFA attempts, and other additive measures) is unaffected, no matter how far back the window reaches.
The limit bites only on summaries that the API itself computes, because the API can only see the last 366.5 days when it does so. The cumulative unique-user columns are the affected case: a count must be computed by the API rather than summed from daily rows (summing daily unique users would count user-days, not distinct people). The mtd_ and ytd_ windows fit inside the retention horizon, but a “since the April 22, 2026 launch” total silently truncates once launch is more than a year in the past (roughly late April 2027). The since_apr22_unique_users fields that previously carried it have therefore been removed from the pipeline.

app_login_counts records a different event type (sso, which IBM Verify files under application usage). Figures from the two tables are therefore not comparable and must never be added together or presented side by side. There is also no per-application breakdown here.

title: ibm_verify.auth_total_logins
text:
Notes
unique_users, failed_logins, and successful_logins are daily values. The mtd_, ytd_, and rolling_365d_ unique-user fields are cumulative and should not be summed across rows; take the latest value within the window instead.
rolling_365d_unique_users is null before 2026-06-13, its implementation date.






Warning



ytd_unique_users and rolling_365d_unique_users may be unreliable. Both are computed by IBM Verify over a longer window than its underlying data retention actually covers, so the figures can undercount, and ytd_unique_users has been seen decreasing from one day to the next. Treat both as estimates only. See Why Unique Users Cannot Be Added Up for detail.


A since_apr22_unique_users field (cumulative distinct users since the April 22, 2026 launch) was previously provided here. It has been removed from the pipeline because the source API retains only the most recent 366.5 days of data, so a since-launch cumulative count cannot be maintained once launch is more than a year in the past. See the retention note on the IBM Verify catalog overview.
When a user signs in to CanadaLogin itself, IBM Verify records each authentication method as a separate event. Entering a username and password followed by a second factor like an OTP counts as two successful events. A mistyped password that is then entered correctly, followed by a correct OTP, counts as three events: two successful and one failed. Both successful_logins and failed_logins are therefore inflated relative to the number of distinct sign-in sessions.
This inflation applies only to signing in to CanadaLogin itself. Reaching an integrated application does not add to these counts at all: it raises an SSO event on app_login_counts instead. CanadaLogin uses the session the person already holds and issues the application a freshly minted assertion or token, so the person enters no password and no second factor.
Summing successful_logins is therefore a misleading indicator of actual user engagement. Instead, use the unique_users field, which is daily active users, and is a measure of the number of users who engaged with the system in a given day.

title: jira.psom_sla
text:
Notes
The four SLAs.

first_response: Jira’s “Time to first response”.
time_to_done: Jira’s “Time to done”, for the whole ticket. It keeps running while the ticket is escalated and pauses while waiting for the customer.
pso_time_to_done: “Time to Done - PSO”, the PSO team’s touchtime. It pauses while the ticket is escalated, or waiting for the customer. It only started on tickets created from about 2026-08-06.
escalated_to_pt: “Escalated to PT”, which runs while the ticket is escalated to the authentication team.

Working time. Goals and elapsed time count working minutes on the SLA’s 09:00 to 17:00 calendar, not wall-clock minutes, so a 40-hour goal is one working week.
Goals vary by ticket. The goal on a clock varies by ticket (for time_to_done, 16, 24, 40 and 72 hours all occur). A breach means the ticket missed its own target. To compare speed across tickets, use elapsed_minutes rather than breached.
Which cycle. A Jira SLA can restart when a ticket is reopened. Each row describes the running cycle if there is one, otherwise the last completed cycle. Earlier cycles are not kept.
Backfilled history (through 2026-09-28). Snapshots are daily from 2026-09-29. Before that they were weekly, on Mondays, and were backfilled from the sla_* columns that psom used to carry. The older snapshots only carry first_response and time_to_done, and only due and breached. There are no rows for the other two SLAs, and goal_minutes, elapsed_minutes and paused are null. breached is null in every row of the 2026-06-30 and 2026-07-06 snapshots, which predate a pipeline fix. It is populated from 2026-07-07 on.

title: Relying Parties
text:
Joining through the lookup
Resolve a source-system name to a relying party by joining on alias, then join rp_id to service for the attributes:
SELECT s.service_name_en,
       sum(a.successful_logins) AS successful_logins
FROM ibm_verify.app_login_counts a
JOIN rp.alias al ON a.application_name = al.alias
JOIN rp.service s ON al.rp_id = s.rp_id
WHERE a.from_date BETWEEN DATE '2026-07-01' AND DATE '2026-07-31'
GROUP BY s.service_name_en
Aggregate after the join, never before. Several IBM Verify application names can map to one service, so a pre-aggregated count keyed on application_name will split a service across its environments.

title: Relying Parties
text:
Data quality
Because the source is a hand-maintained spreadsheet, a few caveats apply to both tables:

The list is not a complete inventory. Services are added when they appear in IBM Verify or analytics data, so a live service with no traffic yet will be missing.
New names need a manual edit. An application name that appears in IBM Verify before someone adds it to the sheet will not resolve, and an inner join will drop its rows without complaint. Left join and check for nulls when you care about coverage.
Free-text columns are unvalidated. service_name_en, service_name_fr, and operator are typed by hand, so expect occasional drift in spelling and spacing. Group by gc_orgid rather than operator.
Neither table keeps history. Each refresh overwrites the previous one, so a service renamed in the sheet is renamed retroactively for every report.

Notes

Upstream monitoring gap (July 28 – September 23, 2026). Automated synthetic probes in cds-snc/status-statut halted during this period due to GitHub Actions workflow execution protections. title: Call Centre
text:
Metrics in this section are calculated from call centre activity and topic data.
Call centre metrics are useful for understanding support demand, service responsiveness, caller wait times, average call duration, and common reasons for contact. The source data is weekly, so these metrics are typically reported at a weekly level or aggregated across weeks.
The relevant call centre tables are:
date_range_start and date_range_end are stored as text, so date-range filters cast them to DATE before comparing to date literals.

title: Call Centre
text:
Activity Metrics
Metrics in this section describe call centre operations, sourced from call_centre.weekly_activity_report.






Metric



Description

Topic Metrics
Metrics in this section describe why people contact the call centre, sourced from call_centre.weekly_topic_dump. Because a single call can generate multiple topic rows, these metrics count topic records rather than distinct calls. Clean statobject before grouping, since it often carries leading, trailing, or repeated whitespace.






Metric



Description

title: Answer Rate
text:
The proportion of accepted calls that were answered by an agent.
This metric is the complement of abandonment and any other non-answered outcomes. It summarizes how much of incoming demand the call centre actually served.

title: Answer Rate
text:
Calculation
Divide the sum of calls_answered by the sum of calls_accepted over the selected reporting period.






NoteExample queries






SQLR


SELECT
    SUM(CAST(calls_answered AS DOUBLE))
        / NULLIF(SUM(CAST(calls_accepted AS DOUBLE)), 0) AS answer_rate
FROM call_centre.weekly_activity_report
WHERE CAST(date_range_start AS DATE) BETWEEN DATE '2026-01-01' AND DATE '2026-05-31';


tbl(con, in_schema("call_centre", "weekly_activity_report")) |>
  filter(
    as.Date(date_range_start) >= as.Date("2026-01-01"),
    as.Date(date_range_start) <= as.Date("2026-05-31")
  ) |>
  summarise(
    answer_rate =
      sum(calls_answered, na.rm = TRUE) /
        sum(calls_accepted, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

title: Answer Rate
text:
Interpretation notes
The rate is a proportion between 0 and 1. A high answer rate with rising delay can still indicate strain: calls are answered eventually, but callers wait longer to reach an agent.

title: Answer Rate
text:
Alternative names

answer ratio
proportion of calls answered
pickup rate
calls answered rate

title: Average Delay
text:
The average delay before calls are answered.
This metric is useful for understanding caller wait times and call centre responsiveness. Like average call length, it should be calculated as a weighted mean to avoid low-volume weeks distorting the result.

title: Average Delay
text:
Calculation
Calculate a weighted average of weekly average delay, weighted by the number of answered calls.






NoteExample queries






SQLR


Weighted average over a period:
SELECT
    SUM(
        CAST(avg_delay_seconds AS DOUBLE)
        * CAST(calls_answered AS DOUBLE)
    )
    / NULLIF(SUM(CAST(calls_answered AS DOUBLE)), 0) AS weighted_avg_delay_seconds
FROM call_centre.weekly_activity_report
WHERE CAST(date_range_start AS DATE) BETWEEN DATE '2026-01-01' AND DATE '2026-05-31';
By week:
SELECT
    date_range_start,
    date_range_end,
    CAST(avg_delay_seconds AS DOUBLE) AS avg_delay_seconds,
    CAST(calls_answered AS BIGINT) AS calls_answered
FROM call_centre.weekly_activity_report
ORDER BY date_range_start;


Weighted average over a period:
tbl(con, in_schema("call_centre", "weekly_activity_report")) |>
  filter(
    as.Date(date_range_start) >= as.Date("2026-01-01"),
    as.Date(date_range_start) <= as.Date("2026-05-31")
  ) |>
  summarise(
    weighted_avg_delay_seconds =
      sum(avg_delay_seconds * calls_answered, na.rm = TRUE) /
        sum(calls_answered, na.rm = TRUE)
  )
By week:
tbl(con, in_schema("call_centre", "weekly_activity_report")) |>
  arrange(date_range_start) |>
  select(
    date_range_start,
    date_range_end,
    avg_delay_seconds,
    calls_answered
  )

title: Average Delay
text:
Interpretation notes
Average delay should be interpreted alongside call volume. A low-volume week can produce unusual wait times that should not dominate the overall result.

title: Average Delay
text:
Alternative names

average wait time
average delay before answer
caller wait time
time to answer
average queue delay

title: Call Topic Share
text:
The percentage of all topic records represented by each call topic.
This is useful for understanding the relative importance of each call driver compared to the overall volume.

title: Call Topic Share
text:
Calculation
Count records by cleaned topic, then divide each topic count by the total count across all topics.






NoteExample queries






SQLR


WITH topic_counts AS (
    SELECT
        REGEXP_REPLACE(TRIM(statobject), '\s+', ' ') AS call_topic,
        COUNT(*) AS topic_count
    FROM call_centre.weekly_topic_dump
    GROUP BY REGEXP_REPLACE(TRIM(statobject), '\s+', ' ')
)

SELECT
    call_topic,
    topic_count,
    CAST(topic_count AS DOUBLE)
        / NULLIF(SUM(topic_count) OVER (), 0) AS topic_share
FROM topic_counts
ORDER BY topic_count DESC;


tbl(con, in_schema("call_centre", "weekly_topic_dump")) |>
  mutate(
    call_topic = str_squish(statobject)
  ) |>
  count(call_topic, name = "topic_count") |>
  mutate(
    topic_share = as.double(topic_count) / sum(topic_count, na.rm = TRUE)
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(topic_count))

title: Call Topic Share
text:
Interpretation notes
Topic share is useful for comparing relative demand across contact reasons. Interpret alongside total call volume.

title: Call Topic Share
text:

share of calls by topic
percentage of calls by reason
topic distribution
call reason mix

title: Calls Answered
text:
The number of calls answered by call centre agents during a reporting period.
This metric is also used as a weighting variable when calculating weighted average call length and weighted average delay.

title: Calls Answered
text:
Calculation
Use calls_answered by reporting period, or sum across periods for a total.






NoteExample queries






SQLR


By week:
SELECT
    date_range_start,
    date_range_end,
    CAST(calls_answered AS BIGINT) AS calls_answered
FROM call_centre.weekly_activity_report
ORDER BY date_range_start;
Total over a period:
SELECT
    SUM(CAST(calls_answered AS BIGINT)) AS total_calls_answered
FROM call_centre.weekly_activity_report
WHERE CAST(date_range_start AS DATE) BETWEEN DATE '2026-01-01' AND DATE '2026-05-31';


By week:
tbl(con, in_schema("call_centre", "weekly_activity_report")) |>
  arrange(date_range_start) |>
  select(
    date_range_start,
    date_range_end,
    calls_answered
  )
Total over a period:
tbl(con, in_schema("call_centre", "weekly_activity_report")) |>
  filter(
    as.Date(date_range_start) >= as.Date("2026-01-01"),
    as.Date(date_range_start) <= as.Date("2026-05-31")
  ) |>
  summarise(
    total_calls_answered = sum(calls_answered, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

title: Calls Answered
text:
Interpretation notes
Calls answered is commonly used as the weighting field when combining weekly average call length or delay values.

title: Calls Answered
text:
Alternative names

answered calls
calls handled
agent-answered calls
completed calls
calls taken by agents

title: Service Level (Answered Within 60s)
text:
The proportion of calls answered within 60 seconds.
This metric is a standard call centre service-level measure of how quickly the queue is cleared. The source data stores only the weekly proportion (pct_answered_within_60s), not the underlying within-60s count, so combine weeks with a weighted average rather than re-deriving from counts.

title: Service Level (Answered Within 60s)
text:
Calculation
Calculate a weighted average of pct_answered_within_60s, weighted by calls_answered.






NoteExample queries






SQLR


SELECT
    SUM(
        CAST(pct_answered_within_60s AS DOUBLE)
        * CAST(calls_answered AS DOUBLE)
    )
    / NULLIF(SUM(CAST(calls_answered AS DOUBLE)), 0) AS service_level_60s
FROM call_centre.weekly_activity_report
WHERE CAST(date_range_start AS DATE) BETWEEN DATE '2026-01-01' AND DATE '2026-05-31';


tbl(con, in_schema("call_centre", "weekly_activity_report")) |>
  filter(
    as.Date(date_range_start) >= as.Date("2026-01-01"),
    as.Date(date_range_start) <= as.Date("2026-05-31")
  ) |>
  summarise(
    service_level_60s =
      sum(pct_answered_within_60s * calls_answered, na.rm = TRUE) /
        sum(calls_answered, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

title: Service Level (Answered Within 60s)
text:
Interpretation notes
The result is a proportion between 0 and 1. Because only the weekly proportion is stored, the weighted average is an approximation of the true within-60s rate, but it is far closer than a simple average of weekly values.

title: Service Level (Answered Within 60s)
text:
Alternative names

service level
SLA
grade of service
percent answered within 60 seconds
speed of answer

title: Google Analytics
text:
Metrics derived from the CanadaLogin GA4 property, in the google_analytics schema. See the Data Catalog for the underlying tables.
Task success rates are computed from GA4 funnels: named, ordered sequences of page or event steps, defined as version-controlled YAML rather than a private GA4 UI exploration. A funnel’s exact steps can change as CanadaLogin’s own pages change, so metrics on this page describe the general calculation and point to that YAML on GitHub as the definitive, current source, rather than hard-coding step names that may already be out of date by the time they’re read.
