title: IBM Verify
text:
Metrics in this section come from IBM Verify, which records two different kinds of event. It raises an authentication event when someone presents an authentication method to CanadaLogin: a password, then a second factor. It raises an SSO event when someone who is already signed in reaches a partner service, and files that one under application usage. These are separate event types, so a figure taken from one is never comparable to a figure taken from the other.
A user signs in to CanadaLogin once and gets a session. Reaching a partner service afterwards does not sign them in again: CanadaLogin uses the session it already holds and issues the partner a freshly minted assertion or token. One sign-in, then as many handoffs as the user needs.
“Sign-in” is prose only. No table counts it, so it is never an output column name or an axis label, and names a metric only where that metric is labelled an estimate.
The relevant IBM Verify tables are:
Internal applications. Internal applications are typically excluded from public-facing adoption metrics. Which ones are internal comes from rp.service.is_internal, resolved to IBM Verify’s application names through rp.alias:
Use the subquery rather than a pasted list, so the classification stays in one place. See the internal applications note in notes.qmd.

The person enters no password and no second factor, which is why these counts are not inflated the way the CanadaLogin-wide authentication events are.

title: IBM Verify
text:
Multi-factor Authentication Metrics
Metrics in this section describe multi-factor authentication (MFA) activity, sourced from ibm_verify.mfa_activity. That table has one row per day per MFA factor (mfa_type) per outcome (result), with the number of attempts in count.
IBM Verify files MFA as a subtype of the authentication event rather than as an event type of its own, so these counts are a slice of the CanadaLogin-wide authentication events, not a separate stream.






Metric

Sign-in MFA Activity by Factor

title: Average Daily SSO Events
text:
The average number of SSO events per day for each application over a selected reporting period.
This metric summarizes daily application usage into a single per-application average value. It is useful for understanding typical daily usage during a launch period, reporting window, or monitoring period.

title: Average Daily SSO Events
text:
Calculation
For each application, calculate the average of total_logins across all daily records in the selected reporting period.






NoteExample queries






SQLR


SELECT
    application_name,
    AVG(total_logins) AS average_daily_sso_events
FROM ibm_verify.app_login_counts
-- set the reporting window; see the timespans note in cookbook/notes.qmd
WHERE from_date BETWEEN DATE '2026-04-22' AND DATE '2026-05-31'
-- to exclude internal applications from adoption reporting, uncomment:
-- AND application_name NOT IN (
--     SELECT al.alias
--     FROM   rp.alias al
--     JOIN   rp.service s ON al.rp_id = s.rp_id
--     WHERE  s.is_internal
-- )
GROUP BY application_name
ORDER BY average_daily_sso_events DESC;


tbl(con, in_schema("ibm_verify", "app_login_counts")) |>
  # set the reporting window; see the timespans note in cookbook/notes.qmd
  filter(
    from_date >= as.Date("2026-04-22"),
    from_date <= as.Date("2026-05-31")
  ) |>
  # to exclude internal applications from adoption reporting, uncomment:
  # anti_join(
  #   tbl(con, in_schema("rp", "alias")) |>
  #     inner_join(tbl(con, in_schema("rp", "service")), by = "rp_id") |>
  #     filter(is_internal) |>
  #     select(application_name = alias),
  #   by = "application_name"
  # ) |>
  group_by(application_name) |>
  summarise(
    average_daily_sso_events = mean(total_logins, na.rm = TRUE)
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(average_daily_sso_events))

title: Average Daily SSO Events
text:
Interpretation notes
The average is taken over the daily rows present for each application in the window, not over every calendar day. If an application has no row on a day with zero activity, that day does not pull the average down, so the figure reflects typical activity on active days.

title: Average Daily SSO Events
text:
Alternative names

average SSO events per day
typical daily usage volume
mean daily SSO event volume
average daily application usage

title: Cumulative Unique Users by Application
text:
The number of distinct users observed for each application over a chosen reporting window: this month or this calendar year.
The cumulative unique-user columns increase or remain stable over time. This metric is closer to “how many distinct people have used the application in this window” than the daily unique user metrics.

title: Cumulative Unique Users by Application
text:
Calculation
Take the latest value of the cumulative unique-user column over the selected window, grouped by application. The window is chosen by which column you read (see the note on reporting timespans):

mtd_unique_users for month-to-date
ytd_unique_users for year-to-date

The WHERE from_date BETWEEN ... bounds set the “as of” reporting date; the most recent row in the window holds the current cumulative total.






Warning



ytd_unique_users may be unreliable. IBM Verify computes it over a longer window than its underlying data retention actually covers, so the figure can undercount and has been seen decreasing from one day to the next. Treat it as an estimate only, and prefer mtd_unique_users where the reporting question allows. See Why Unique Users Cannot Be Added Up for detail.


A since_apr22_unique_users column (cumulative distinct users since launch) was previously available but has been removed; see the data retention note.






NoteExample queries






SQLR


Month-to-date:
WITH ranked AS (
    SELECT
        application_name,
        from_date,
        mtd_unique_users,
        ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
            PARTITION BY application_name
            ORDER BY from_date DESC
        ) AS rn
    FROM ibm_verify.app_login_counts
    WHERE from_date BETWEEN DATE '2026-06-01' AND DATE '2026-06-08'
    -- to exclude internal applications from adoption reporting, uncomment:
    -- AND application_name NOT IN (
    --     SELECT al.alias
    --     FROM   rp.alias al
    --     JOIN   rp.service s ON al.rp_id = s.rp_id
    --     WHERE  s.is_internal
    -- )
)

SELECT
    application_name,
    mtd_unique_users
FROM ranked
WHERE rn = 1
ORDER BY mtd_unique_users DESC;
Year-to-date:
WITH ranked AS (
    SELECT
        application_name,
        from_date,
        ytd_unique_users,
        ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
            PARTITION BY application_name
            ORDER BY from_date DESC
        ) AS rn
    FROM ibm_verify.app_login_counts
    WHERE from_date BETWEEN DATE '2026-01-01' AND DATE '2026-06-08'
    -- to exclude internal applications from adoption reporting, uncomment:
    -- AND application_name NOT IN (
    --     SELECT al.alias
    --     FROM   rp.alias al
    --     JOIN   rp.service s ON al.rp_id = s.rp_id
    --     WHERE  s.is_internal
    -- )
)

SELECT
    application_name,
    ytd_unique_users
FROM ranked
WHERE rn = 1
ORDER BY ytd_unique_users DESC;


Month-to-date:
tbl(con, in_schema("ibm_verify", "app_login_counts")) |>
  filter(
    from_date >= as.Date("2026-06-01"),
    from_date <= as.Date("2026-06-08")
  ) |>
  # to exclude internal applications from adoption reporting, uncomment:
  # anti_join(
  #   tbl(con, in_schema("rp", "alias")) |>
  #     inner_join(tbl(con, in_schema("rp", "service")), by = "rp_id") |>
  #     filter(is_internal) |>
  #     select(application_name = alias),
  #   by = "application_name"
  # ) |>
  group_by(application_name) |>
  slice_max(
    from_date,
    n = 1,
    with_ties = FALSE
  ) |>
  select(
    application_name,
    mtd_unique_users
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(mtd_unique_users))
Year-to-date:
tbl(con, in_schema("ibm_verify", "app_login_counts")) |>
  filter(
    from_date >= as.Date("2026-01-01"),
    from_date <= as.Date("2026-06-08")
  ) |>
  # to exclude internal applications from adoption reporting, uncomment:
  # anti_join(
  #   tbl(con, in_schema("rp", "alias")) |>
  #     inner_join(tbl(con, in_schema("rp", "service")), by = "rp_id") |>
  #     filter(is_internal) |>
  #     select(application_name = alias),

title: All MFA Activity by Factor
text:
The volume of MFA attempts broken down by factor type, with each factor’s share of total activity. This is the platform-wide view: it covers every factor type the system records, including the internal and administrative factors (kq, totp, qr, ibm_verify_push) and the email_otp factor used only to validate emails at sign-up. For usage restricted to the factors the public can sign in with, see Sign-in MFA Activity by Factor.
This metric shows which second factors are exercised across the whole platform. Historically the mix has been dominated by sms_otp and email_otp. Passkeys (fido2) became generally available to the public on 2026-07-06, so fido2 volume is expected to grow from that point, while factors such as totp, kq, qr, voice_otp, and ibm_verify_push continue to see little use.

title: All MFA Activity by Factor
text:
Calculation
Sum count grouped by mfa_type, then divide each factor’s total by the overall total to get its share. As with MFA Authentications, de-duplicate before counting: OTP factor types (sms_otp, email_otp, voice_otp) record both a sent event and a subsequent success/failure event for the same challenge, so only the sent row is counted for these; non-OTP factor types (fido2, kq, totp, ibm_verify_push) have no sent event and are counted through their success/failure rows. Without this, OTP factors are roughly double-counted relative to non-OTP factors.






NoteExample queries






SQLR


SELECT
    mfa_type,
    SUM(count) AS mfa_authentications,
    CAST(SUM(count) AS DOUBLE)
        / NULLIF(SUM(SUM(count)) OVER (), 0) AS factor_share
FROM ibm_verify.mfa_activity
-- set the reporting window; see the timespans note in cookbook/notes.qmd
WHERE from_date BETWEEN DATE '2026-01-01' AND DATE '2026-05-28'
  -- de-duplicate OTP challenges: count only "sent" for OTP types, and
  -- "success"/"failure" for non-OTP types (which have no "sent" event).
  AND (
    result = 'sent'
    OR (
      result IN ('success', 'failure')
      AND mfa_type NOT IN ('sms_otp', 'email_otp', 'voice_otp')
    )
  )
GROUP BY mfa_type
ORDER BY mfa_authentications DESC;


otp_types <- c("sms_otp", "email_otp", "voice_otp")

tbl(con, in_schema("ibm_verify", "mfa_activity")) |>
  # set the reporting window; see the timespans note in cookbook/notes.qmd
  filter(
    from_date >= as.Date("2026-01-01"),
    from_date <= as.Date("2026-05-28"),
    # de-duplicate OTP challenges: count only "sent" for OTP types, and
    # "success"/"failure" for non-OTP types (which have no "sent" event).
    result == "sent" |
      (result %in% c("success", "failure") & !mfa_type %in% otp_types)
  ) |>
  group_by(mfa_type) |>
  summarise(
    mfa_authentications = sum(count, na.rm = TRUE)
  ) |>
  mutate(
    factor_share =
      as.double(mfa_authentications) / sum(mfa_authentications, na.rm = TRUE)
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(mfa_authentications))

title: MFA Success Rate by Factor
text:
The MFA success rate broken down by factor type, so that factors can be compared against one another.
This metric is useful for spotting whether one second factor is notably easier to clear than another. Because the rate is calculated per attempt, a factor that users frequently mistype before getting right (common with OTP factors) shows a lower rate, which is the friction signal you want when comparing ease of use.

title: MFA Success Rate by Factor
text:
Calculation
Within each mfa_type, divide the sum of count where result = 'success' by the sum of count where result is 'success' or 'failure'. As with the overall MFA Success Rate, sent rows are excluded from both the numerator and the denominator because they are not outcomes. mfa_attempts is the denominator (successes plus failures) and is reported alongside the rate so that low-volume factors, whose rates are noisy, can be discounted.
Note that mfa_attempts here counts success and failure events only. It is not the de-duplicated usage volume reported by All MFA Activity by Factor, which counts sent events for OTP factors instead.






NoteExample queries






SQLR


By factor:
SELECT
    mfa_type,
    SUM(count) AS mfa_attempts,
    CAST(SUM(count) FILTER (WHERE result = 'success') AS DOUBLE)
        / NULLIF(SUM(count), 0) AS mfa_success_rate
FROM ibm_verify.mfa_activity
-- set the reporting window; see the timespans note in cookbook/notes.qmd
WHERE from_date BETWEEN DATE '2026-01-01' AND DATE '2026-05-28'
  -- exclude "sent" rows; success rate is calculated from outcome events only.
  -- including "sent" would inflate the denominator and deflate the rate.
  AND result IN ('success', 'failure')
GROUP BY mfa_type
ORDER BY mfa_attempts DESC;
By factor and week:
SELECT
    date_trunc('week', from_date) AS week_start,
    mfa_type,
    SUM(count) AS mfa_attempts,
    CAST(SUM(count) FILTER (WHERE result = 'success') AS DOUBLE)
        / NULLIF(SUM(count), 0) AS mfa_success_rate
FROM ibm_verify.mfa_activity
-- set the reporting window; see the timespans note in cookbook/notes.qmd
WHERE from_date BETWEEN DATE '2026-01-01' AND DATE '2026-05-28'
  AND result IN ('success', 'failure')
-- date_trunc('week', ...) anchors each bin to its Monday
GROUP BY date_trunc('week', from_date), mfa_type
ORDER BY week_start, mfa_type;


By factor:
tbl(con, in_schema("ibm_verify", "mfa_activity")) |>
  # set the reporting window; see the timespans note in cookbook/notes.qmd
  filter(
    from_date >= as.Date("2026-01-01"),
    from_date <= as.Date("2026-05-28"),
    # exclude "sent" rows; success rate is calculated from outcome events only.
    # including "sent" would inflate the denominator and deflate the rate.
    result %in% c("success", "failure")
  ) |>
  group_by(mfa_type) |>
  summarise(
    mfa_attempts = sum(count, na.rm = TRUE),
    mfa_success_rate =
      sum(if_else(result == "success", as.double(count), 0), na.rm = TRUE) /
        sum(count, na.rm = TRUE)
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(mfa_attempts))
By factor and week:
tbl(con, in_schema("ibm_verify", "mfa_activity")) |>
  # set the reporting window; see the timespans note in cookbook/notes.qmd
  filter(
    from_date >= as.Date("2026-01-01"),
    from_date <= as.Date("2026-05-28"),
    result %in% c("success", "failure")
  ) |>
  # floor_date(..., "week") translates to Athena's date_trunc('week', ...),
  # which anchors each bin to its Monday
  mutate(week_start = floor_date(from_date, "week")) |>
  group_by(week_start, mfa_type) |>
  summarise(
    mfa_attempts = sum(count, na.rm = TRUE),
    mfa_success_rate =
      sum(if_else(result == "success", as.double(count), 0), na.rm = TRUE) /
        sum(count, na.rm = TRUE)
  ) |>
  arrange(week_start, mfa_type)

In the weekly view, the first and last weeks of the reporting window are usually partial (the window rarely starts or ends on a Monday), so treat boundary weeks with caution when comparing trends.

WHERE rn = 1

title: SSO Success Rate by Application
text:
The proportion of SSO events that succeeded, broken down by application.
This is the success rate of the handoff to an application, not of anyone signing in. It helps isolate problems to a specific application: one with a markedly lower success rate than its peers is worth investigating for integration or configuration issues.

title: SSO Success Rate by Application
text:
Calculation
Divide the sum of successful_logins by the sum of all attempts (successful_logins + failed_logins) over the selected reporting period, grouped by application.






NoteExample queries






SQLR


SELECT
    application_name,
    CAST(SUM(successful_logins) AS DOUBLE)
        / NULLIF(SUM(successful_logins + failed_logins), 0) AS sso_success_rate
FROM ibm_verify.app_login_counts
-- set the reporting window; see the timespans note in cookbook/notes.qmd
WHERE from_date BETWEEN DATE '2026-01-01' AND DATE '2026-05-28'
-- optionally filter out internal applications; see the internal applications
-- note in cookbook/notes.qmd
  AND application_name NOT IN (
      SELECT al.alias
      FROM   rp.alias al
      JOIN   rp.service s ON al.rp_id = s.rp_id
      WHERE  s.is_internal
  )
GROUP BY application_name
ORDER BY sso_success_rate DESC;


internal_apps <- tbl(con, in_schema("rp", "alias")) |>
  inner_join(tbl(con, in_schema("rp", "service")), by = "rp_id") |>
  filter(is_internal) |>
  select(application_name = alias)

tbl(con, in_schema("ibm_verify", "app_login_counts")) |>
  # set the reporting window; see the timespans note in cookbook/notes.qmd
  filter(
    from_date >= as.Date("2026-01-01"),
    from_date <= as.Date("2026-05-28")
  ) |>
  # optionally filter out internal applications; see the internal applications
  # note in cookbook/notes.qmd
  anti_join(internal_apps, by = "application_name") |>
  group_by(application_name) |>
  summarise(
    sso_success_rate =
      sum(as.double(successful_logins), na.rm = TRUE) /
        sum(successful_logins + failed_logins, na.rm = TRUE)
  ) |>

It counts a different IBM Verify event type from the CanadaLogin-wide authentication success rate, so the two are not comparable.

title: SSO Events by Application
text:
The total number of SSO events recorded for each application over a selected time period.
IBM Verify raises an SSO event when someone who is already signed in reaches an application. It uses the CanadaLogin session they already hold, so the person enters no password and no second factor. This metric is useful for understanding usage volume across CanadaLogin-integrated applications. It counts events, not people: one person reaching an application several times contributes several events.
The source column is total_logins, but the event it counts is what IBM Verify calls an SSO event, part of application usage.

This counts events, not people. Use this metric when the question is about system usage or activity volume. Use unique user metrics when the question is about reach.
These are a different IBM Verify event type from the CanadaLogin-wide authentication events, so never add the two together or present them side by side as comparable figures. Unlike the authentication events, SSO events are not inflated by second factors, because reaching an application uses the session the person already holds rather than asking them to authenticate again.

FROM ibm_verify.auth_total_logins

WHERE from_date BETWEEN DATE '2026-01-01' AND DATE '2026-05-28';

FROM ibm_verify.auth_total_logins
-- set the reporting window; see the timespans note in cookbook/notes.qmd
WHERE from_date BETWEEN DATE '2026-01-01' AND DATE '2026-05-28'
-- date_trunc('week', ...) anchors each bin to its Monday
GROUP BY date_trunc('week', from_date)
ORDER BY week_start;


Overall:
tbl(con, in_schema("ibm_verify", "auth_total_logins")) |>
  # set the reporting window; see the timespans note in cookbook/notes.qmd
  filter(
    from_date >= as.Date("2026-01-01"),
    from_date <= as.Date("2026-05-28")
  ) |>
  summarise(
    total_authentication_events = sum(failed_logins + successful_logins, na.rm = TRUE)

By week:
tbl(con, in_schema("ibm_verify", "auth_total_logins")) |>

title: SLA PSO Time-to-Done Breach Rate
text:
The proportion of PSOM tickets that missed the “Time to Done - PSO” SLA, based on the latest snapshot.
This metric reflects how well the PSO team is resolving tickets within the agreed timeframe, counting only the time the ticket is with that team. Unlike the whole-ticket SLA Time-to-Done Breach Rate, its clock pauses while the ticket is escalated. Like that SLA, it also pauses while waiting for the customer. Only tickets where the SLA clock started are included; tickets with no clock are excluded.

title: SLA PSO Time-to-Done Breach Rate
text:
Calculation
From jira.psom_sla, filter to the most recent date partition, to sla = 'pso_time_to_done', and to rows where breached is not null (i.e., the clock started). Divide the count of rows where breached is true by the total count of those rows.






NoteExample queries






SQLR


SELECT
    COUNT(*) AS total_sla_tickets,
    SUM(CASE WHEN breached THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS breached_count,
    CAST(SUM(CASE WHEN breached THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS DOUBLE)
        / NULLIF(COUNT(*), 0) AS breach_rate
FROM jira.psom_sla
WHERE date = (SELECT MAX(date) FROM jira.psom_sla)
  AND sla = 'pso_time_to_done'
  AND breached IS NOT NULL;


psom_sla <- tbl(con, in_schema("jira", "psom_sla"))
latest_date <- psom_sla |> summarise(d = max(date, na.rm = TRUE)) |> pull(d)

psom_sla |>
  filter(
    as.Date(date) == as.Date(latest_date),
    sla == "pso_time_to_done",
    !is.na(breached)
  ) |>
  summarise(
    total_sla_tickets = n(),
    breached_count    = sum(as.integer(breached), na.rm = TRUE),
    breach_rate       = sum(as.integer(breached), na.rm = TRUE) / as.double(n())
  )

title: SLA PSO Time-to-Done Breach Rate
text:
Interpretation notes
The rate is a proportion between 0 and 1. Tickets whose clock never started (null breached) are excluded from both numerator and denominator. Check total_sla_tickets to understand the sample size underlying the rate.
This clock only started on tickets created from about 2026-08-06, and the older snapshots have no pso_time_to_done rows, so the sample is smaller than for the other SLAs. The goal is set per ticket and counted in working hours (09:00 to 17:00), so a breach means the ticket missed its own target.
A ticket that is still open and inside its goal is recorded as not breached (false), the same as a ticket that met the SLA. The rate on a live snapshot is therefore a lower bound: some of those open tickets may still breach before they are resolved. It is most meaningful once the snapshot’s tickets are largely resolved.

title: Additional Notes
section: Daily unique users are not the same as period unique users
text:
Daily unique users are not the same as period unique users
Summing daily unique users gives a measure of user-days, not distinct people over the full period.
For distinct people over a longer period, use a cumulative unique user field such as mtd_unique_users or ytd_unique_users.
For a plain-language explanation of why the daily figures cannot be added, and why no unique-user count exists for an arbitrary window, see Why Unique Users Cannot Be Added Up.

title: Additional Notes
section: Metrics can be reported over different timespans
text:
Metrics can be reported over different timespans
Most metrics are meaningful over more than one window. The three standard reporting windows are month-to-date, year-to-date, and since the April 22, 2026 public launch. How you select a window depends on the kind of metric.
Additive metrics (sign-ins, MFA attempts, success rates, averages) are computed by aggregating daily rows, so the window is just the date bounds in the WHERE from_date BETWEEN DATE '<start>' AND DATE '<end>' clause. The same query covers any window; only the start date changes:

Month-to-date: first of the current month (for example, 2026-06-01)
Year-to-date: 2026-01-01
Since launch: 2026-04-22

Set the end date to the reporting date.
Cumulative unique-user metrics cannot be derived by filtering a date range, because summing daily unique_users counts user-days, not distinct people. Instead, pick the pre-computed column that matches the window and take its latest value:

Month-to-date: mtd_unique_users
Year-to-date: ytd_unique_users

Never sum these cumulative columns across rows.






Warning



ytd_unique_users (and the rolling_365d_unique_users field used elsewhere) may be unreliable. IBM Verify computes both over a longer window than its underlying data retention actually covers, so the figures can undercount and ytd_unique_users has been seen decreasing from one day to the next. Treat both as estimates only. See Why Unique Users Cannot Be Added Up for detail.


There is no cumulative since-launch column. The since_apr22_unique_users field that previously provided it has been removed: the cumulative count is computed by the IBM Verify API, which sees only the most recent 366.5 days of source data, so a since-launch total silently truncates once launch is more than a year in the past. The mtd_ and ytd_ windows are unaffected because they fall inside that horizon.
This limit does not affect the additive metrics above. Those are aggregated from the daily rows we store on our side, which are retained beyond a year, so a date-bounded since-launch window over an additive metric stays correct however far back it reaches. See the data retention note in the catalog.

title: Additional Notes
section: Weighted averages should be used for call centre averages
text:
Weighted averages should be used for call centre averages
When calculating average call length or average delay across multiple weeks, use a weighted average based on calls_answered.
A simple average of weekly averages may give too much influence to low-volume weeks.

title: Additional Notes
section: Internal applications should usually be excluded from external adoption reporting
text:
Internal applications should usually be excluded from external adoption reporting
Which applications count as internal is recorded in rp.service.is_internal, not in this document. Resolve it through rp.alias, which maps the application names IBM Verify and Google Analytics use back to a single service:
SELECT al.alias
FROM   rp.alias al
JOIN   rp.service s ON al.rp_id = s.rp_id
WHERE  s.is_internal
Query the list rather than pasting it into a filter. A service is reclassified by editing the source spreadsheet, and a query holding its own copy of the list will not notice. The same subquery works as a NOT IN in SQL and as an anti_join() in dbplyr; both forms appear in SSO Events by Application.
Whether to exclude internal applications at all depends on the reporting question.

title: Mean Time to Resolution
text: The average time, in minutes, from when an incident is detected to when it is fully resolved.

title: Mean Time to Resolution
text:
Calculation
Average mttr_detected_resolved (minutes from detected_at to resolved_at, precomputed in the table) across the incidents whose detected_at falls in the reporting window, from sre.mttr_current. Because the incident timestamps are stored as America/Toronto strings rather than native dates, the window casts the YYYY-MM-DD prefix of detected_at to a DATE instead of filtering a from_date column. Unresolved incidents have a null mttr_detected_resolved and are excluded from the average.
To break the figure out for service-level reporting, group the same average by severity.






NoteExample queries






SQLR


Overall:
SELECT
    AVG(mttr_detected_resolved) AS mean_time_to_resolution
FROM sre.mttr_current
-- set the reporting window on detected_at; see the timespans note in cookbook/notes.qmd
WHERE CAST(substr(detected_at, 1, 10) AS DATE) BETWEEN DATE '2026-01-01' AND DATE '2026-06-26';
By severity:
SELECT
    severity,
    AVG(mttr_detected_resolved) AS mean_time_to_resolution
FROM sre.mttr_current
-- set the reporting window on detected_at; see the timespans note in cookbook/notes.qmd
WHERE CAST(substr(detected_at, 1, 10) AS DATE) BETWEEN DATE '2026-01-01' AND DATE '2026-06-26'
GROUP BY severity
ORDER BY severity;


Overall:
tbl(con, in_schema("sre", "mttr_current")) |>
  # set the reporting window on detected_at; see the timespans note in cookbook/notes.qmd
  filter(
    as.Date(str_sub(detected_at, 1, 10)) >= as.Date("2026-01-01"),
    as.Date(str_sub(detected_at, 1, 10)) <= as.Date("2026-06-26")
  ) |>
  summarise(
    mean_time_to_resolution = mean(mttr_detected_resolved, na.rm = TRUE)
  )
By severity:
tbl(con, in_schema("sre", "mttr_current")) |>
  # set the reporting window on detected_at; see the timespans note in cookbook/notes.qmd
  filter(
    as.Date(str_sub(detected_at, 1, 10)) >= as.Date("2026-01-01"),
    as.Date(str_sub(detected_at, 1, 10)) <= as.Date("2026-06-26")
  ) |>
  group_by(severity) |>
  summarise(
    mean_time_to_resolution = mean(mttr_detected_resolved, na.rm = TRUE)
  ) |>
  arrange(severity)

title: Mean Time to Resolution
text:
Interpretation notes
The figure is in minutes; divide by 60 for hours. It is a mean, so a single very long incident can pull it up sharply, especially given how few incidents there are in any window. Read it alongside the incident count, and consider a median or a Sev1-only cut when one outlier dominates.
The window is anchored on detected_at, so an incident counts in the period it began, even if it was resolved in a later period. severity is unvalidated free text in the source sheet, so the grouped view reflects whatever values were typed (expect the occasional typo or spacing drift).

title: Site Response Time
text: The average HTTP response time for each monitored CanadaLogin site, aggregated over rolling windows from five-minute ping data.

title: Site Response Time
text:
Calculation
Filter to the most recent date partition and read the precomputed rolling-window response time columns from sre.uptime_summary. Each response_*_ms column is the mean response time in milliseconds over all five-minute pings in the named window.
For a single-ping point-in-time reading (not an average), use sre.uptime_timeseries.response_ms instead.






Warning



Upstream monitoring gap (July 28 – September 23, 2026): External synthetic health checks in cds-snc/status-statut halted during this ~8-week window. Because zero pings were executed, average latency collapsed to response_day_ms = 0 (a physical impossibility for real HTTP traffic).

When querying historical response time trends or averages, filter out unmonitored days using WHERE response_day_ms > 0.









NoteExample queries






SQLR


Latest snapshot, all sites, all rolling windows:
SELECT
    slug,
    lang,
    status,
    response_day_ms,
    response_week_ms,
    response_month_ms,
    response_year_ms,
    response_alltime_ms
FROM sre.uptime_summary
WHERE date = (SELECT MAX(date) FROM sre.uptime_summary)
ORDER BY slug;
Trend over time, weekly average response time for a specific site:
SELECT
    date,
    response_week_ms,
    response_alltime_ms
FROM sre.uptime_summary
-- set the reporting window; see the timespans note in cookbook/notes.qmd
WHERE slug = 'canada-login-website-en'
  AND CAST(date AS DATE) BETWEEN DATE '2026-01-01' AND DATE '2026-06-30'
  -- exclude dates where upstream monitoring was inactive
  AND response_day_ms > 0
ORDER BY date;


Latest snapshot, all sites, all rolling windows:
uptime_s <- tbl(con, in_schema("sre", "uptime_summary"))
latest_date <- uptime_s |> summarise(d = max(date, na.rm = TRUE)) |> pull(d)

uptime_s |>
  filter(as.Date(date) == as.Date(latest_date)) |>
  select(slug, lang, status, response_day_ms, response_week_ms,
         response_month_ms, response_year_ms, response_alltime_ms) |>
  arrange(slug)
Trend over time, weekly average response time for a specific site:
tbl(con, in_schema("sre", "uptime_summary")) |>
  # set the reporting window; see the timespans note in cookbook/notes.qmd
  filter(
    slug == "canada-login-website-en",
    as.Date(date) >= as.Date("2026-01-01"),
    as.Date(date) <= as.Date("2026-06-30"),
    # exclude dates where upstream monitoring was inactive
    response_day_ms > 0
  ) |>
  select(date, response_week_ms, response_alltime_ms) |>
  arrange(date)

title: Site Response Time
text:
Interpretation notes
Response times are averages computed from all 288 five-minute pings in the window. Single-measurement spikes are smoothed out. During outage periods, pings that time out contribute high response times or are excluded depending on the upptime implementation, so treat response time trends during known outage windows with caution.
During the July 28 – September 23, 2026 monitoring outage, response_day_ms was recorded as 0, serving as a sentinel value. Failing to filter out these dates (response_day_ms > 0) will artificially drag down historical average latency figures.

title: Why Unique Users Cannot Be Added Up
text:
A unique-user figure counts people, not sign-ins. That makes it behave differently from most numbers in this cookbook. This page explains the two rules that follow, why they exist, and what to ask for instead.
The short version:

title: Why Unique Users Cannot Be Added Up
section: One week, two ways of counting
text:
One week, two ways of counting
Here is a week of sign-ins by five people. A dot means that person signed in that day.



A grid of five people against seven days, with a dot on each day a person signed in. The daily count of people is 2, 2, 2, 2, 2, 1, 1. Adding those gives 12, but there are only 5 names.


Both totals are correct. They answer different questions.

12 is the number of person-days: the number of times someone showed up on a given day. Amira counts five times because she came on five days.
5 is the number of people. Amira counts once no matter how many days she came.

The daily unique-user figure is the “people that day” row. Adding that row up gives person-days, not people. So a report that says “we had 12 unique users this week” would be wrong. The true figure is 5.

title: Why Unique Users Cannot Be Added Up
section: Why the totals do not add
text:
Why the totals do not add
Adding two unique-user figures only works if nobody appears in both. In practice, the regular users appear in every period, and they get counted again each time.



Two overlapping circles. The Monday circle holds Ben and Amira, the Tuesday circle holds Amira and Chloe. Amira sits in the overlap.


To get the true figure you need to know who was in the overlap. That means knowing which people were behind each count, and we do not have that information.
The same thing happens across applications. Someone who uses two integrated applications is one unique user for CanadaLogin overall but appears in each application’s own count. Adding up the applications’ figures over-counts them, and the overall CanadaLogin figure will always be smaller than that sum.

title: Why Unique Users Cannot Be Added Up
section: What we keep, and what we do not
text:
What we keep, and what we do not
IBM Verify, the service behind CanadaLogin sign-in, is the only system that knows who signed in. It keeps that per-person record for 90 days, then deletes it.
Our data warehouse never receives the per-person record at all. That is a deliberate choice, required by the security and privacy rules CanadaLogin operates under. Each day, IBM Verify counts up the day’s activity and hands us the finished numbers: how many people signed in that day, and how many distinct people have signed in so far this month. We store the numbers. We do not store, and cannot look up, who was behind them.



A timeline showing IBM Verify holding the per-person record for only the last 90 days, above three rows showing what the warehouse keeps: a figure per day, a figure per calendar month, and a custom window marked as not stored and not rebuildable.


This is why a unique-user count exists only for the windows we asked for in advance. If nobody asked for “April 22 to June 30” before those days happened, the count was never made. We cannot make it now, because we hold no names to count, and after 90 days neither does IBM Verify.

title: Why Unique Users Cannot Be Added Up
section: What you can and cannot ask for
text:
What you can and cannot ask for







Question
Can we answer it?




How many people signed in yesterday?
Yes. We have a figure for every day.


How many people signed in in July?
Yes. We have a figure for every calendar month.


How many people signed in on average per day in July?
Yes. Averaging the daily figures is fine; it is adding them that misleads.


How many people signed in from April 22 to June 30?
No. That window was not set up in advance, and it cannot be rebuilt.


How many people signed in in the second quarter?
No. A quarter is three monthly figures, and monthly figures cannot be added.


How many people used Application A or Application B?
No. Each application has its own figure, and the two overlap.


How many people have signed in this year?
Not reliably. See the next section.



Person-days, the “12” above, is a legitimate measure on its own. It is the right denominator for a rate such as calls per active user, where each day’s activity should count. Just do not present it as a number of people.

title: Why Unique Users Cannot Be Added Up
text:
Year-to-date and 365-day figures
The tables also carry a year-to-date figure and a rolling 365-day figure. Both are calculated by IBM Verify over a window longer than the 90 days of per-person data it holds, so they cannot be right. The year-to-date figure has been seen going down from one day to the next, which a true cumulative count cannot do. Do not quote either figure until the pipeline is fixed. The daily and monthly figures are unaffected because both windows fit inside 90 days.
